on both experimental and theoretical frameworks. We derive a simplified model 
to describe these phenomena and illustrate its relevance with specific 
examples, highlighting the value of understanding and applying this model in 
the development of advanced materials with improved durability and strength.

A lower bound has been established for a Gaussian free field configured within a polygon with specified boundary lengths, resulting in the discovery that each boundary component is driven by a specific Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) which coalesces into a larger component, while also applying a diffusion process which reaches a single, unified, largest component, underlying this field can be decomposed into multiple non-crossing SLEs, with their driving functions derived from joint distributions of Schur and log-laplace processes, this field's distribution is proven to be equivalent to samples obtained from stochastic difference equations, which encode discrete samples from the Seiberg-Witten theory in two-dimensional Yang-Mills theory.

We introduce a novel method for solving three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with periodic initial conditions, leveraging the maximum principle and an innovative spatial approximation technique based on the maximum norm. To achieve this, the nonlinear term is redefined using an exact, nonlinear operator that satisfies the maximum principle. Subsequently, the semidiscrete and fully discrete approximations are developed through time integration with the implicit Crank-Nicolosn scheme, yielding a new solution at each step by addressing a particular elliptic equation. It is demonstrated that both the semidiscrete and fully discrete solutions provide a rigorous and unconditionally stable approximation to the exact solution by proving that the approximation errors remain contained within specific function spaces governed by the maximum norm. Moreover, numerical experiments confirm the method's ability to deliver optimal convergence rates for the spatial and temporal discretization.

The growing promise of quantum computers relies heavily on the need for efficient and scalable error correction methods. Current methods employ auxiliary qubits, error correction codes, and interactive proofs, but these approaches are still in development. In order to bridge this gap, we propose a classic verification system that uses minimal auxiliary resources. Our proposed system checks quantum computations by using a compact number of auxiliary qubits, enabling the creation of deep circuits for verifying complex computations. The depth of our proposed error checking circuit depends only on logarithmically scaling factors, and not on the computation being verified. Moreover, our approach significantly simplifies classical processing, reducing verification errors to near-instantaneous checkable states. The efficacy of our proposed system is demonstrated through successful error correction of deep circuits up to 5000 gates in just 5000 gates.

A blockchain network is capable of maintaining data integrity due to its inherent structure, yet its direct access to off-chain data is limited. To resolve this, a case study is proposed, focusing on establishing a connection between a blockchain ecosystem and real-world data through a model of an Internet of Things (IoT) enabled blockchain framework. This framework is essential for verifying the authenticity of blockchain stored data by cross-checking it with off-chain data, and also ensures data usage is by authorized users only. The framework is implemented by utilizing an oracle that validates the consistency of blockchain and off-chain data, and a data usage oracle that grants access based on predetermined data usage policies. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated in the context of the FoodFi platform, a blockchain-based system for overseeing the traceability of the food supply chain. The proposed solution is evaluated by running performance tests on an Ethereum test network and analyzing its computational cost, transaction processing time as well as its scalability and tolerance to various network attacks.

Creative digital modeling holds significant value in various industries, such as entertainment and design, but its application in biology remains underutilized due to the complexity of organic forms. To address this limitation, our study proposes a novel approach for visualizing live cells in two dimensions using a combination of neural networks and statistical analysis. By training a generative model on neural networks, we can reconstruct the meaningful relationships within the data and capture the process distributions associated with the cell's life cycle. We validate the effectiveness of our proposed method through experiments, which also reveal its potential to provide insights into the cell's behavior and inner workings.

Individuals experiencing print-related disabilities face significant challenges when attempting to access documents formatted in traditional PDFs. Their reliance on screen readers to navigate digital content proves ineffective due to the limited functionality of these devices in displaying document contents. The paper outlines several use cases highlighting the difficulties screen readers impose on print-disabled individuals and presents several design suggestions for enhancing screen reader capabilities to better serve this population.

Recently, multiple pretraining approaches for the linguistic understanding task have been proposed, each having their own merits and demerits. XLNet unifies various pretraining objectives under a single generalized autoregressive model. Within this framework, XLNet can naturally incorporate aspects of other methods and address their limitations. Additionally, thanks to its autoregressive nature, new joint likelihood loss can be introduced and two key issues with masked language models are resolved. XLNet's performance is superior to recent advancements in the realm of Sanak and ELNet.

The detection of atmospheric signatures in exoplanets relies heavily on precise low-resolution spectroscopy during transit events. However, stellar activity can distort these signatures and mimic the presence of atmospheric features in young planets. This study examines how stellar active regions affect atmospheric measurements and whether high-resolution spectroscopy can help mitigate these effects, focusing on a "typical" planet undergoing transit with a spotless stellar spectrum and a stellar active region. By analyzing atmospheric features in the star's disc and active region, the research quantifies activity-induced distortions in transit spectra and shows that, for certain atmospheric features, the activity impact can be detected using high-resolution spectroscopy. Consequently, high-resolution spectroscopy can assist in distinguishing atmospheric features from the effects of stellar activity in certain scenarios.

We are investigating how the presence of degenerate marked points on a Riemann surface can be represented by constant curvature metrics with singularities. These singularities have specific strength that corresponds to the severity of each marked point. The purpose of this note is to demonstrate the existence of such metrics for combinations of negative integer strengths that have a positive sum. The proof involves applying the continuity method to a type of nonlinear elliptic equation that incorporates degenerate Frobenius conditions. Our approach allows the development of sequences of smooth approximations to the target metric, thus ensuring the obtained metric has a desired level of smoothness.

In nature, animals have adapted to move through water by power swimming and on the surface by running along the water's skin, but the transition in movement dynamics between the two environments is not well understood. This lack of understanding is especially critical for centipedes, a group that showcases remarkable diversity in weight, with some species capable of running on water while others are too heavy and must move through the water. Our research reveals that as centipedes become lighter, a shift in movement patterns occurs, and this shift is marked by a change in the way they move their legs. Specifically, heavier species move through water in a particular rhythm, but lighter species switch to this same rhythm when running on the surface, and this change in rhythm occurs when the centipedes move from breaking waves in the water to capillary waves on the surface. By using 3D tracking technology and underwater videos, we were able to measure the centipedes' movement and calculate the force required to move through water and on the Froude number. Our findings suggest that the centipedes' movement is controlled by the interplay between their body dynamics and the waves they create, and that this interplay changes as the species gets lighter. Ultimately, our research provides new insights into the movement dynamics of centipedes and could help us better understand the movement patterns of other creatures that move through water and on the surface.

The study of planetary formation relies on modeling asteroid collisions that can be enhanced by employing high-resolution, adaptive grid techniques. This research focuses on developing a framework for adiabatic fluid simulations based on the Navier-Stokes equations. This approach utilizes high-order methods within an adaptive grid framework. The method's feasibility is demonstrated through a series of tests on the turbulent transmission of tsunamis generated by asteroid collisions. The initial simulations involved a coarse grid with approximately 10 million cells, revealing that the adaptive framework can effectively trace the movement of tsunamis in complex environments. This traceability is confirmed through comparisons to earlier models and laboratory experiments, revealing discrepancies of about 10-15% in the coast line. The research also revealed that refining the grid up to one million cells per collision significantly improves the simulations, particularly in cases of large collisions. However, the rapid increase in computational costs poses a limitation. To address this issue, we developed a multi-physics approach that allows for a detailed simulation of the early stages of the collision, including the coast line, by breaking down the complex scenario into simpler sub-scenarios. This approach, combined with the adaptive framework, enables us to simulate the transmission of tsunamis with up to approximately 5 million cells. The research highlights the potential challenges in accurately modeling the coast line of a planet, particularly in cases where adaptive methods are used to simulate the transmission of tsunamis.

In a recent study, we analyzed the properties of a specific set of galaxies observed in the early data from the JWST's NIRCam and NIRSpec instruments. This sample consists of 28 highly luminous galaxies at extremely high redshifts, ranging from 2.8 to 8.5, which were previously identified using Spitzer Space Telescope data and marked as peculiar due to their low optical brightness. We discovered that the new JWST data reveals these galaxies to be predominantly star-forming systems, which contrasts sharply with their 2014-2016 spectral data. This significant revision of their properties can be attributed to the enhanced sensitivity and broader wavelength coverage of JWST's instruments, particularly for the galaxies at the highest redshifts. Our findings imply that previous spectral analyses of these galaxies were likely compromised by inaccurate continuum placement and line misidentification.

Researchers are currently exploring whether a certain invariant, proposed earlier by the authors, could lead to a new quantum Yang-Mills equation. This paper investigates whether a analogous equation could have significance in seven-dimensional general relativity. The authors discover that a newly constructed equation in seven-dimensional spacetime reveals interesting topological properties and potential implications for understanding gravitational black holes and the universe's overall structure.

In the channels of food processors and mills, the crushing or grinding of materials occurs at low speeds, where rotating impellers create shocks and intense forces within a confined space. Similar conditions can be found in biological environments, such as jaw movements, and industrial die design for polymer processing, where entangled polymer chains experience compression between plates with oscillating motions. These systems can be compared to disks that are restricted from rotating along their axis, resulting in two-dimensional clogged disks with particles confined within a confined space. By simulating the movement of each particle, we can model the system's dynamics and analyze the effects of pressure and displacement on the material within the disk. Our simulations reveal alternating sequences of compression and displacement that occur as a result of the mechanical forces applied to the material.

This research examines precipitation patterns in the global context during El Ni\~n~o phases.
Using ground-based observations from the Climate Research Unit precipitation dataset,
it's discovered that certain regions like the tropics of South America, Southern Africa,
and parts of the Arctic experience a significant shift in precipitation patterns.
In contrast, other areas like Southeast Asia, Australia, and Central America show more pronounced changes.
Our analysis reveals a distinct climate response to a specific type of El Ni\~n~o - the
central type - which is characterized by heating in the Pacific Ocean's central region.
This type of El Ni\~n~o - central type - induces a significant shift in precipitation patterns in areas like Southeast Asia and Australia.
On the other hand, a different type of El Ni\~n~o - which is associated with elevated precipitation - is characterized by heating in the Pacific Ocean's eastern region.
Our findings also highlight how certain types of El Ni\~n~o events, like those seen in recent decades, are more likely to occur and could have a significant impact on certain regions like the tropics of South America, which typically experience cooling in precipitation patterns during the central type of El Ni\~n~o - central type of El Ni\~n~o - central type of El Ni\~n~o - central type of El Ni\~n~O events.

The structure transformation during crystallization is complex and intricate, which research on indium antimonide crystals has shown can lead to unique patterns in scattered light. These variations can manifest as structural instabilities in the top layers of the crystal, resulting from the non-uniform growth process. By analyzing these inconsistencies in the light scattering data, it's possible to gain insights into the structure evolution of the crystal, including the dynamics of dislocation movements. Specifically, the intensity of the scattered light can indicate the extent of these movements, which can be influenced by internal stresses and defects within the crystal.

This research introduces modified, age-structured models of population growth to examine the influence of environmental pollution on the demographic patterns of a population. To account for environmental toxicity, we introduce a parameter that affects age-specific mortality rates of organisms. We develop models based on the von Foerster and Bernoulli equations to simulate various population dynamics, such as those of birthrate-controlled and foerster-controlled populations. We then analyze the existence, stability, and asymptotic behavior of these populations over time. Additionally, we investigate whether our model predictions align with the law of population conservation. We conclude by testing the feasibility of finding unique weak solutions to these model equations through numerical simulations, using age-specific birth and death rates as boundary conditions.

Substructural logics have seen a significant increase in the number of novel systems in recent times. Researchers within the substructural community are actively developing contraction extensions for these systems to address existing weaknesses. This paper examines the impact of the contraction operator on the decidable properties and computational complexities of the $M$-logic and the Minkowski system, as well as their respective contraction expansions. Our analysis reveals that the contraction expansions of the $M$-logic and the Minkowski system retain the same upper decision complexity as their parent systems, while the decision lower complexity remains unchanged, indicating the preservation of these properties upon the expansion.

We introduce a novel technique for expanding classifiers, particularly in complex data distributions. This dynamic learning framework is based on a representation learned continuously from data sources of increasing difficulty, arranged in a hierarchical, exponentially weighted map derived from a simplified model of information demand. This unique approach enables the classifier to adapt and improve its knowledge as it progresses through various levels of data complexity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, HyperExpan, against conventional static learning models and other dynamic approaches, and showcase its potential applications, including progressive expansion of image classification datasets across multiple stages.

This research examines how electric fields impact the stability and interactions of various molecular pairs. We've discovered that the effect of an electric field on the interaction strength of these pairs is not consistent. While some pairs, such as CO2 and H2O, experience a significant increase in interaction strength, others like benzene and ethane show themselves to be less affected. Our findings suggest that the behavior in this context is largely dependent on the characteristics of the molecules involved and the nature of the electric field present. We've also identified that this phenomenon is closely related to the orientation of molecular pairs and that some pairs, such as CO2 and H2O, show themselves to be more affected by the electric field when compared to others. These findings have significant implications for the design and functionality of molecular systems that operate in electric fields.

The effective use of Industry 4.0 technologies relies heavily on accurately processing complex data from interconnected machines, products, and systems. Our research delves into addressing the uncertainty inherent in Industry 4.0 data through the integration of probabilistic scheduling methods. We address the issue of ambiguity in real-time data by applying contextual clues to its interpretation, making it suitable for industrial environments. To illustrate our approach, we applied a stochastic scheduling model to simulated Industry 4.0 data to enhance the understanding of ambiguity in a manufacturing setting.

In recent years, significant effort has been devoted to establishing formal specifications for cyber physical systems. One specification language in particular, linear temporal logic with signals and their levels, has gained widespread adoption. However, traditional approaches focus on verifying whether a given specification is satisfied by a system, disregarding the degree of satisfaction. This limits their applicability to cyber physical systems due to their inherent uncertainty and potential for violating specifications by an arbitrary margin. In order to overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages a temporal logic to segment the parameter space and employ a metric to quantify robustness across each segment. Our proposed framework encompasses various well-known satisfaction metrics and can accommodate novel, customizable metrics tailored to the specifics of individual systems. Our solution's efficiency is demonstrated through real-world examples, and its potential for practical application is highlighted in the context of designing controllers.

Accelerometer-based networks have the potential to detect a vast number of small objects, such as grains of sand, pebbles, boulders, and even mountains. By analyzing motion patterns and utilizing machine learning or physics-based methods, these devices can pinpoint the shape, size, and mass of moving objects. A key limitation, however, is that accelerometers cannot effectively detect stationary objects, slow-moving entities, or those impacted by external factors that mask their movement signals. To overcome this obstacle, we investigate the use of advanced signal processing techniques to uncover subtle signs of object motion and develop new search methods capable of identifying objects that go unnoticed due to environmental interference. Our simulations demonstrate the utility of these methods in identifying objects as small as a single grain of sand, as well as those weighing over 100 kilograms obscured by the impact of wind, seismic activity, animal disturbances, and more. By combining these novel approaches with data from seismic and satellite imagery, we are able to reconstruct plausible trajectories for some of these hidden objects.

Consider a nonlinear diffusion equation on complete manifolds, with a given measure in terms of a weight function.  We develop an analogue of Gol'dstein's representation for such manifolds under specific conditions, under which we also derive estimates for the first derivative of the solution with respect to initial data.  We also establish a comparison principle and prove the existence of a Laplacian diffusion approximation for such manifolds.

The morphological properties of compact radio sources in the cosmic web are studied by analyzing their brightness profiles. Using a stacked analysis, researchers investigate how these features change with angular size. By combining radio sources into groups based on their flux, researchers observe a correlation between their physical properties and surface brightness. However, a more detailed analysis of high-flux sources is hindered by limitations in angular resolution provided by the FAST telescope. Consequently, a stack of 1000 Faint MACHO candidates, aimed at sources in the 5-10 arcsec range, is performed and compared to other datasets. The results indicate a peak surface brightness of 3.5 Jy/arcsec^2, with a significant correlation between the gradient of brightness and angular size. High-flux sources exhibit a notable deviation from these trends, with a peak maximum surface brightness of 12 Jy/arcsec^2, particularly for sources smaller than 10 arcsec. The distribution of peak surface brightness for all sources is also examined, with a notable shift observed in high-flux sources towards lower values. These findings provide new insights into the physical properties of cosmic sources, with a particular emphasis on their compactness.

Concealed Markov models (CMMs) are a useful tool for analyzing an agent's decision-making process in response to observations, enabling researchers to identify and stop any potential internal state that might be considered inadmissible. A new subclass of these models, known as abstract concealed markov models (ACMMs), is proposed where transitions are independent of specific inputs. This study demonstrates a method for describing the set of all feasible ACMMs based on an observation space and associated penalties, which acts like a functor that maps these models to a monadic structure over the free commutative semigroup of non-negative values. This method ensures that the least comprehensive set of ACMMs produced can define the required quantitative information flow analysis.

Nonlinear spatially extended systems exhibit coherent dynamics governed by state variables and diffusion processes, leading to statistical nonlocality where system states influence each other over significant distances. Statistical nonlocality arises when systems with localizing mechanisms and conservative systems exhibit a measurable correlation between past and present states at various spatial points. We introduce and explain the concept, and its experimental and numerical detection through the nonlocal autocorrelation function, and demonstrate its evolution and saturation during a specific transition and equilibrium state in both systems. Moreover, we show that system states can be reconstructed based on nonlocal information and its implications for understanding the dynamic behavior of conservative systems.

We've developed a unified framework to study flexible scattering, where the dimensionality of the scattering system can vary continuously. By employing Regge theory, we find that dimensions less than 3 are associated with unconfined systems, while those above 4 are completely non-interacting. Our analysis shows that the interesting physics occurs in the range of 4 > d > 3, where dimensions close to 3 show signs of confinement but are not fully confined, and dimensions close to 4 exhibit unbinding but not fully unbinding. Our findings shed new light on the scattering physics, particularly near the lower boundary, where we predict new phenomena such as superconvergent scattering and non-zero mean first passage times. We also predict a superconvergent spectrum in the unbound state, consisting of a dense set of states with a different density compared to the bulk. These predictions can be verified by studying weakly interacting gases in dimensions just below 4, where we predict unbounded convergence timescales, even at a non-zero temperature. Our research reveals a rich and intricate structure of phenomena that can emerge as one moves along the dimensionality axis.

This work examines how the Casimir effect influences blackbody radiation pressure within a spherical cavity of large size and minimal thickness. A non-relativistic quantum field is considered in a frame of reference where potential energy is constant, and a small perturbation is applied. By solving the resulting Schrödinger equation for bound states, we find an increased state density, yielding an equation similar to the ideal gas law. Specifically, we calculate the pressure of photons confined within a cavity of these characteristics. Assuming pressure changes are negligible relative to thermal energy, we determine thermal energy and entropy as a function of this perturbation using standard statistical ensembles in equilibrium. We find that both thermal properties exhibit altered behavior of a linear nature due to the Casimir effect, contradicting a hypothesis proposed in a previous study and demonstrating that the Casimir effect can contribute to thermal properties of blackbody radiation in equilibrium.

Protecting against location tracking is crucial for individuals, businesses, and government agencies. Existing methods focus on ensuring anonymity through techniques like using decoy locations, but few address the problem of tracking over time based on historical movement data. This research introduces a new system designed to balance an user's need for privacy with their tracking utility across multiple time periods, relying on a conditional prior of historical movement patterns. A variational inference method generates a reliability threshold for predictions from this prior, allowing it to adapt to an user's growing understanding of their movement data. As a result, sampling from this prior beyond the reliability threshold provides significant privacy benefits. We tested this novel approach on real-world movement data and found that it substantially reduces the risk of accurate tracking, even when using real-world movement data priors.

The widespread use of 3D point cloud localization systems relies heavily on Place Recognizer (PR) modules to efficiently sift through large maps, but this process is often computationally expensive and time-consuming due to the extensive size of the map. To address this limitation, we developed the NDT-Transformer, an innovative architecture that integrates the Partial NDT algorithm which depictions rather than poses it optimizes, into a large-scale 2D and 3D point cloud localization framework. This new system, built upon the Transformer architecture, utilizes a Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) module to leverage the relationships between NRT depictions. As a PR, the NDT-Transformer can quickly identify areas of the map that potentially contain the correct location by using a small point cloud query and depositions, allowing for the elimination of areas that are certainly not the correct location in large maps, such as those with hundreds of kilometers, such as. In the case of 2D and 3D localization, the NDT-Transformer can find the correct NRT depiction with a few top-k most probable ones, and then use optimization to find the correct pose. In the case of 2D and 3D localization, the NDT-Transformer can find the correct pose in the case of noise. In the case of 2D and 3D localization, the NDT-Transformer can find the correct pose in the case of noise.

Research using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging relies heavily on connecting brain regions through graph analysis, facilitated by connectivity measures, such as correlation coefficients, derived from spatially and temporally based data analysis. Our study focuses on developing a framework for evaluating a network of correlated brain regions by incorporating probabilistic measures, specifically the statistical strength, which quantifies the confidence in connectivity, in addition to predicting connections between regions based on small-scale imaging features. We applied our multi-objective method to a comprehensive dataset of 1,590 subjects from the 1000 Functional Brain Project to identify factors influencing a region's connectiveness and identify those traits that consistently predict correlations across different brain regions. Our results show that the statistical strength of connections at the cortical surface is generally predicted with a high degree of accuracy, as evidenced by the substantial number of correctly identified correlations out of a total possible number. We further demonstrate that the statistical strength can effectively capture both structural integrity, as measured by the diffusion of water molecules along neural pathways, as well as individual differences in correlation coefficients.

In networks where nodes can only signal by listening or transmitting, and cannot distinguish between silence and a message, we investigate the energy-efficient communication problem.  We focus on two tasks: node identification and short message transmission. We adapt the concepts of identification codes and their variant, the prefix property, to this context, introducing the term 'silent-prefix property' for transmission. We develop a classification system for these properties based on their duration. Our key findings involve introducing 'codes with a single period' for set sizes up to six, and 'codes with a single half-period' for set sizes up to five, all while minimizing energy consumption through the minimization of zero counts. This leads to an optimal solution where the set size is no more than five, with each transmission lasting at most one bit. However, this is not feasible when the set size exceeds five. We explore the trade-off between the duration of periods and half-periods and the minimum transmission length, identifying patterns in (0,1)-codes with unit weights. We find two distinct types of codes: long periodic codes and those with a single half, characterized by the transmission length. We introduce the term 'n-identifying codes' and investigate their minimum transmission length, varying the number of silent transmission periods and half-periods. We identify minimum lengths for periodic identifying codes and discuss two key issues: the minimum number of half-periods required for any set size n, and the minimum number of silent transmission periods required when employing periodic identifying

Positional encodings, prevalent in numerous domains, efficiently capture the dynamic and sequential aspects of data. However, in mixed language settings, the approach falls short due to the inconsistent and irregular usage of languages. We present a segment, marked by a shift in language, which we define as a 'Transition Point' and utilize it to encode segments in a position-dependent manner. We define the 'Transformer Transition Point encoder' (PESTO), which utilizes a posited transition point as a means to encode positions in models like BERT and T5. PESTO's 20 selected transitions outperform other leading positional encodings across various tasks, encompassing posited and actual T5 models. We further establish the PESTO framework, enabling the efficient construction of custom-made positional encodings that cater to the intricacies of mixed language settings.

The high-temperature superconductivity properties of H$_3$S hydride were explored
across a range of pressures between 140 and 230 GPa, incorporating
electron-phonon coupling corrections via quasi-particle dispersion. For each
pressure condition, the Debye temperature was evaluated using specific heat
capacity, leading to a precise measurement of Debye mass. By applying an
isotope correction using the Isotope Effect Law, we found the Debye mass to be
insensitive to isotopes, resulting in a critical temperature that follows
an inverse relationship with the isotopes. For the first time, we deconvoluted
the effects of electron-phonon coupling coupling constants, Debye mass, and
isotope dependence on Tc superconducting parameters. Notably, we found a
critical role of the van Hove singularity near the Fermi level near 200 GPa,
influencing Tc's isotope dependence through enhanced electron-phonon coupling
constants. This study provides the first comprehensive understanding of Tc's
behavior across different isotopes and pressures in H$_3$S, in addition to
its deconvoluted isotope dependence and pressure dependence.

As environments become more populated with obstacles, finding feasible paths to navigate becomes increasingly challenging. We propose a novel approach that strategically condenses the navigable space by utilizing corridor-like structures to determine the existence of non-collision paths when standard path-finding algorithms fail to produce results. Our method ensures that if a path is found within these artificially narrowed limits, it will also be feasible for the original problem, and it also guarantees path existence in cases where the navigable space is very small or non-circular. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through simulations in 2D and 3D environments with dynamic obstacles.

Visual localisation is a fundamental and extensively researched computer vision task that involves determining a camera's position and orientation within a 3D scene. Although numerous methods have been proposed, they frequently require extensive hand-crafted design expertise and extensive training processes to achieve optimal results. This paper presents a approach to visual relocalisation that incorporates 3D scene structural information to position the camera accurately. In our approach, a compact surfel database is used to represent 3D scene geometry, and this database is automatically generated through a SLAM algorithm. This allows for reduced dependency on manual feature engineering and improved performance. Furthermore, we propose a new method for learning visual features using a CNN architecture, and demonstrate its effectiveness through extensive experiments on multiple datasets.

In the context of Multiuser MIMO (MIMO-MU) systems, the task of determining the best user selection and precoding techniques simultaneously is crucial. This issue has been reformulated as an optimization problem that can be effectively addressed by applying a specialized reconstruction technique based on the Group LASSO approach, which facilitates variable separation and promotes sparse solutions. The proposed interpretation demonstrates that this reconstruction technique can accurately account for power constraints and leads to an efficient, sub-optimal solution with a low computational cost. Through simulations, the performance of the suggested method is validated by comparing it with other approaches, demonstrating that it can achieve performance on par with, and in some cases surpassing, other methods while maintaining a significant reduction in complexity.

We prove that the tropical semiring of rational functions of degree $k$, generated from the standard semiring of variables, is itself finitely generated. This corresponds to the fact that the tropical arc space of a projective scheme of dimension $d$ over a field, when viewed through its associated tropical arc semiring, possesses a finite set of generators over the tropical semiring. As a result, the tropical arc space of such a projective scheme, when embedded into a projective space of dimension $d$, becomes quasi-affine when embedded sufficiently deeply. Furthermore, when the scheme is smooth, this embedding allows for a finite set of rational functions to generate the tropical arc space, which in turn allows for pre-images of sufficiently pre-images of sufficiently deep embeddings to recover full arc spaces over the tropicalization of the base field. This result also allows for a re-proof of a known theorem, specifically, that for a smooth curve, when embedded sufficiently deeply, its tropicalization recovers the tropicalization of its associated tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of its tropicalization of

This brief note focuses on a specific counterexample previously established by D. Aisner, D. Pollett, and R. Zelenko (DarExAmMa, 2021) and a related finding by AISner and Zelenko (arXiv, 2019), highlighting the potential for non-uniform application of Keyex in general Theorems. In contrast, we establish that for M/M/2-type Q-processes, Keyex-uniform applicability is attainable. Moreover, we establish that for Q-processes exhibiting a specific structural characteristic (specifically those of M/M/x-type), Keyex-uniform applicability can be achieved, even when the convergence rate is inverse-proportional to $\sqrt{n}$.

We have defined a link $L$, a specific 6-component link that can be converted into the Hopf link $H$ by adding four components, by taking the connected sum of three copies of the Borromean rings along with their mirror image. It has been established that there is a state-sum Vassiliev invariant of order three that distinguishes $L$ from $H$, initially by providing a simple combinatorial explanation of the Bar-Natan and Stoltzfus Vassiliev characteristics, and then by presenting an alternative derivation that associates a graphical basis element with a flat connection and demonstrates its non-vanishing property.

The connection between phenomena of quasi-particle excitations and nematic order in
the quasi-layered ferropnictides is still unclear. A notable feature of nematic
superconductors is an order parameter, which is invariant under rotations but broken
by, displaying spontaneous behavior below a certain critical temperature. This
behavior often precedes superconductivity and may also arise in the normal state. In
the case of LiFeAs, a type-nematic superconductor, a proposed explanation attributes
nematicity to the behavior of quasi-particles in the normal state. Our research, based
on a theoretical model of LiFeAs's electronic structure, aims to test the validity of
the quasi-particle origin hypothesis for nematicity. By analyzing the behavior of
nematic susceptibility, a key marker for this phenomenon, in the normal state, we
found that the quasi-particle origin hypothesis fails to provide a satisfactory
explanation for nematicity in LiFeAs, as the calculated temperature dependence does
not align with the experimental findings. Instead, we suggest that nematic order in
LiFeAs arises due to structural asymmetry in the normal state, and its disappearance
in the superconducting state results from a transition to a more symmetric state.

The median global fit results from the latest runs of I, II and III have been utilized to establish the global fit results for various flavor observables under the two Higgs doublet model. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the global fit results from a subsequent run of the IV framework with a heavy scalar mass of $M_H \approx 500$ GeV and $\sin\zeta \approx 0.01$ have global fit results that align with the SM. Notably, the global fit results for $\zeta_H$ within the 2HDM span a broad range across the I-XY models.

The underlying cause of self-assembly lies in basic physical principles that dictate how particles behave. However, conventional simulation methods based on established physics often neglect potential discoveries in self-organizing properties. In contrast, neural network-based approaches can learn and discover novel rules but require extremely computational resources when dealing with complex many-body systems. Taking into account the strengths of both methods, a new framework utilizing neural network-controlled particle dynamics has been proposed. This method, which combines computational efficiency with the ability to discover new self-assembly mechanisms, has been successfully applied to model systems consisting of magnetic dipoles. Through comparison with established physical laws, it demonstrates the capability to not only replicate results obtained from standard simulations, but also to utilize its learned self-assembly knowledge to improve control and discover new mechanisms that could be exploited in future research.

Our anomaly analysis of the quantum spacetime manifold, specifically chiral QED and QCD, is robust against perturbations, such as the introduction of Dirac fermions with arbitrary charges or colors. The anomaly in the 11-dimensional parity invariant spacetime can be characterized by an anomaly polynomial in six dimensions. The analysis shows that the anomaly cannot be canceled by adding Dirac fermions, leading to implications that the quantum spacetime cannot be conformally invariant. The study of topological phases in Dirac fermions coupled to U(1) gauge fields reveals phases characterized by non-trivial boundary conditions for the 10-dimensional spacetime. The topological phases can be further modified by coupling to a background spin connection to establish a non-trivial boundary in the 11-dimensional spacetime.

This study examines the solvability of the three-dimensional steady Navier-Stokes equations in periodic domains in the context of critical Besov spaces. We demonstrate that in this setting, both the pure and inhomogeneous equations can be ill-defined. We establish a precise ill-posedness result for an initial value problem linked to the pure equation. We show that in the relevant critical Besov spaces, a solution to the problem with a small, high-frequency initial data can exhibit a solution with unbounded oscillations. We further show that a solution to an inhomogeneous problem with a div-zero initial data has an unbounded solution, given suitable initial data. We highlight the importance of div-zero conditions in the context of incompressible fluid dynamics equations. We adapt key concepts from Fourier analysis, including the construction of specific sequences and the use of cut-off functions, for the relevant applications.

The properties of magnons in antiferromagnetic insulators are studied under various temperatures and magnetic fields. A recent finding suggests that magnons experience a significant increase in effective mass due to electron interactions and thus are significantly compressed by thermal energy. Our research demonstrates how this thermal compression affects the magnon dynamics, notably resulting in a significant shift in their position and a significant increase in dispersion width. To model this phenomenon, we developed a model that accounts for interactions between electrons and magnons at equilibrium. A key outcome of this research is the prediction of a specific relationship between thermal compression and magnon dispersion width which can be observed in certain materials like Yttrium Iron Garnet and Croped Manganese Oxide. These research findings can be verified through direct measurements of magnon distributions and spectra at various temperatures and magnetic fields, thus providing an experimental validation of the theory. Moreover, our research provides a new perspective on previously observed anomalies in magnon dispersion in these materials, and suggests that these phenomena can be used to create new technologies for manipulating magnons.

This paper offers two novel cryptographic systems built on Loidreau's scheme, which involve incorporating two extra layers of protection. Firstly, we examine the vulnerabilities of Loidreau's scheme against attacks by Welch and Juillard, and then present modifications to bolster it. Secondly, we apply an equivalent by linear Gaussian noise in Loidreau's framework, which also suffers from a particular type of attack, and then alterations are proposed to mitigate it. Both modified systems seem to retain a comparable level of security while presenting simpler overall complexities.

Lexicons, as a means to encode word knowledge, have long been employed in NLP.
However, manual curation is a laborious process. Consequently, one might consider
automating this curation through self-supervised learning methods like dict-BERT,
which incorporates lexicons derived from lemmatization rules. In this work, a
new dict-BERT model, based on the BERT architecture, is proposed. By utilizing
English morphological analysis, lexicons are automatically generated, and the dict-BERT
pre-training process follows the BERT paradigm. Results indicate that dict-BERT's
embeddings surpass those of BERT across multiple tasks, with notable improvements
observed in POS tagging and sentiment analysis. Furthermore, dict-BERT's efficacy
is highlighted through post-training analysis.

To validate the application of topological data analysis in bioinformatics, we investigate a basic model of a complex. Specifically, we examine the asymptotic behavior as the number of data points, n, approaches infinity, for the minimal spanning acycles and persistence diagrams of n points, lines, and triangles in R^3, generated by a stochastic process, according to the Lebesgue measure. In the process, we develop a concept of a good mass partition to prove that the normalized length of the minimal spanning acycles converges almost surely, to a constant that represents the Lebesgue measure of a good mass partition's partition elements. Furthermore, this constant corresponds to a specific value of the 1-Wasserstein distance between two randomly generated measures, that are chosen according to the good mass partition, that partition the space of R^3. In the case of persistence diagrams, using numerical simulations, we show that their distribution converges, by demonstrating that their empirical distributions converge, in the sense of stochastic convergence, for the 1-Wasserstein distance.

A novel method for analyzing and attacking the privacy of data verticals in a federated learning setup, where a horizontal partitioning exists, is presented. A pragmatic approach to assaults is employed, highlighting two novel vertical-level pragmatic assault techniques: (i) sample inference attack and (ii) joint local model inference attack. These methods exploit local update vectors to recover sample labels and encode labels, thereby compromising data confidentiality. To create pragmatic assaults, we integrate the success rates of these attacks with existing cumulative and iterative attacks on client updates. An extensive experiment conducted on three benchmark datasets demonstrates that, under the adaptive hyperparameter method, the proposed cumulative and iterative attacks can successfully compromise data confidentiality even when combined with pragmatic attack techniques.

Dark matter is one of the most significant challenges in particle physics and cosmology. The 2016 CMS findings have suggested possible connections between dark matter and heavy flavor decays, specifically in the production of antibaryons, which could be verified through future particle collider and LHCb experiments. To better understand these processes, researchers have started applying the light-cone sum rules (LCSR) method to calculate the relevant distribution amplitudes (DA). To build a solid foundation, this paper aims to develop synthesis rules for the photon's coupling to a proton and an antidoublet, drawing on the principles of quark and diquark correlations learned from the rules governing the proton's coupling to a photon. The paper provides an in-depth explanation of the calculation process and its implications for DA modeling.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to urban defense management by presenting a game-inspired resource allocation system in the event of simultaneous attacks on a city's social and cyber infrastructure. We integrate elements from contemporary board games like Tabletop Defense and Relic Run, merging them with theoretical resource management strategies that draw from the Schelling's differential game model of combat. To simulate realistic assault scenarios, we employ a game-theoretic optimization technique utilizing the min-max strategy for predicting potential social disruptions. Our proposed city defense management model serves as a technical framework for tackling multiple concurrent threats while efficiently deploying limited resources. Our experimental results showcase the versatility and adaptability of our approach across various levels of complexity, demonstrating its capability to effectively neutralize social, cyber, and physical threats in a city environment.

A low-momentum field can cause a Schwarzschild black hole to transition into a thin black hole with a chamber, and this process occurs instantly, maintaining the thermodynamic equilibrium between the two phases due to the zero thermal properties of the matter involved. Conversely, when a high-temperature black hole's chamber collapses, it forms a low-momentum particle, and this particle can eventually evolve into a transitioning thin black hole. Furthermore, our analysis explores the thermal dynamics of the transitioning black holes, and we also model the heat transfer process between the high-temperature black hole's remnant and the universe using a simulated low-temperature heat bath, and we investigate how the transition black hole evolves into a thin black hole under these conditions.

In the realm of information retrieval, particularly for noisy documents, existing approaches have been ineffective. To address this, a novel approach is introduced that involves a data retrieval process utilizing bag sampling. Additionally, a classification network with cluster-wise loss is developed to identify document ranking signals. Moreover, a two-stage training framework with signal amplification is proposed to enhance the performance of noisy documents in information retrieval. Experiments conducted on the BEIR dataset demonstrate the superiority of this approach over state-of-the-art methods, with specific evaluations on the CLIQR and FEVER datasets.

Recent advancements in pseudo-labeling have enabled learning with minimal human guidance. However, when applied to complex tasks like graph classification within the semi-supervised learning framework, current pseudo-labeling methods face significant challenges. First, they often result in inaccurate pseudo-labels, leading to detrimental semi-supervised learning that hinders the learning process of both active and passive approaches. Second, existing graph classification methods heavily rely on first-order information within limited labeled data, causing them to fail in capturing intricate second- or higher-order node relationships. To address these limitations, we introduce the concept of pseudo-graphs, which enables the identification of more reliable pseudo-labels and sophisticated first-order node information. Furthermore, we propose Enriched Pseudo-Labeling Graph Semi-Supervised Learning (EPLGSS) to leverage pseudo-graphs in enhancing supervised graph representation learning, ultimately aiming to generate more precise pseudo-labels and superior pseudo-first-order node information. To validate the efficacy of our framework, we incorporate it into the widely used Pseudo-Labeling Self-Training with Consistency Regularization (PLSC) method and demonstrate through comprehensive experiments on 11 real-world datasets that it consistently surpasses state-of-the-art benchmarks across various evaluation metrics, particularly when limited labeled data is available.

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in AWAKE's 2022 experiment can identify WKB-based track models, including parametric resonances, through energy distribution analysis of photons produced during loop trajectories of wakefield-driven plasma bubbles. Simulation results using PLUTOS and Plasmaweb confirm the feasibility of observing these resonances in PLUTOS designs, andplasmaw2 is a C++ code thatplutos2's PLUTOS runs augment to analyze additional track models' results , including plasmaw2.

This paper introduces novel techniques for creating scaled-up and reliable versions of differential privacy (DP) tree learning methods. First, we outline a framework to construct and validate private decision trees using statistical tools, ensuring accurate predictions for a given training set while protecting user data. Second, we design efficient algorithms to break down large training sets into smaller chunks that can be processed in parallel, creating distributed and verifiable trees without compromising privacy. Finally, our approach experiments these methods on real datasets, comparing their performance to existing global DP tree learning techniques to ensure the creation of high-quality models even in a decentralized environment.

The Bregman divergences, or Bregman distances, are differences between a strictly concave function and its a convex counterpart, and R\'enyi divergence is a generalization of the well-known Kullback-Leibler divergence within the Bregman divergences family.  A reduced R\'enyi divergence has been shown to be useful for quantifying the sufficiency of statistical data and can be optimized using Bregman proximal gradient methods.  In this study, we investigate a series of regularized Bregman divergences for bivariate normal distributions by employing Bregman proximal gradient methods, and we further extend this to multivariate distributions and further extend to higher dimensions.  In addition, we further extend to higher dimensions.

This article explores using Bayesian models to predict outcomes in multivariate classification graphs based on observational data. Specifically, it focuses on interactive digraphs representing multiple, dependent categorical variables. An extension of traditional Bayesian models, this work introduces methods for modeling interactive digraphs with potential temporal components and existing background information. The main challenge lies in efficiently exploring the complex space of these graphs during model selection. An existing method involves enumerating all potential graphs, but this is computationally infeasible due to the vast number of options. Rather than enumerating, this research introduces a promising framework that systematically selects a manageable set of models and provides a probabilistic method for evaluating their relative fit. An application of this approach is demonstrated, predicting multiple variables simultaneously from election data in Norway over six decades.

This paper develops a novel damping mechanism known as damped inertial dynamics with vanishing Tikhonov regularization. This mechanism is the limiting form of the damped inertial dynamics balancing a strongly coercive vector field. The regulation term is parameterized by a monotone operator A and a continuously decreasing function μ, representing the trade-off between the monotone operator and the function, which converges to zero as time approaches infinity. The main achievement of this paper lies in the demonstration of the trajectory's strong convergence towards x*(A,0), the solution to the variational inequality <Ax, x*>, where x* is the solution's corresponding value and it particularly applies when the solution's corresponding value, denoted by x*, lies in the null space of operator A, resulting in strong convergence towards the minimal norm solution, i.e., x*(0), under specific conditions. Additionally, this paper examines the convergence rate of ∥x'(t)∥ and ∥Ax'(t)∥ and develops tools to analyze the convergence rate of ∥x'(t)∥.

Our research focuses on investigating variations in the trajectories followed by autonomous wall-following robots as starting positions of obstacles are shifted. These known starting positions are intentionally altered to examine the effect of this shift on the robots' distance from the wall and the angle at which they follow the wall. This study was conducted in a simulated environment and real-life settings within a lab, and the data collected was analyzed using a simple statistical method, the Fourier transform, to identify the starting position that causes the most noticeable variation in the robots' trajectories. The chosen statistical method enabled us to determine the optimal starting position that maximizes the effect of the shift. The chosen starting position in both the simulation and the lab was 50 cm, and the outcome of the optimization process was an 85 cm increase in starting position that resulted in a more pronounced variation in trajectory, which could be utilized for the purpose of exploring the environment through leveraged learning. This study was designed as a foundational experiment for leveraged learning, a concept that we have previously proposed, and lays the groundwork for more advanced research in this area in the future.

We analyze the microwave conductivity of thin superconducting films that exhibit
a certain degree of disorder, which causes the formation of extended potential
barriers within the normal state. These barriers prevent the supercurrent from
disrupting the phase coherence, allowing for the coexistence of vortex excitations
and long-range order, even at extremely low frequencies and high temperatures.
To investigate this, we develop a theoretical model that takes into account the
glide of vortices over the barrier landscape under high current densities,
demonstrating a transition from metallic to insulating behavior. Moreover,
our model predicts a sharp change in conductivity when the density of vortices is
close to a critical value, either increasing or decreasing the conductivity
significantly, depending on its proximity to the percolation threshold. These
theoretical findings are consistent with the experimental observations made on
highly doped superconducting materials, specifically those with defects of a specific
size, as well as with the superconducting mechanism driven by kinetic energy.

This passage discusses a non-smooth mean curvature flow, arising from a lim process, where the mean curvature is replaced with a more robust, anisotropic version. Focusing primarily on two dimensions, the text examines the properties of this flow, its relation to other problems such as curvature driven flows and crystal growth, as well as research questions in the field.

The rapidly growing field of robotics has primarily focused on enabling robots to perform tasks such as picking objects and manipulating items, yet these capabilities fall short when confronted with deformable objects like plants and plants' living spaces. Since plants' shapes rely heavily on their growth environment, shaped by their owners, they're effectively controlleable by their operators through the planting, molding, and pruning process. To further bridge the gap between robotics and adaptability, researchers propose GrowSpace, the first simulator designed specifically for plant deformability, incorporating photogrammetry and procedural generation techniques, and presenting multiple challenges in plant Deformation, Discovery, and Growth manipulation.

Using the fusion theory of Liouville conformal field theory, we develop a geometric method to define and study conformal loop ensembles SLE$_{6}$, highlighting the conformal structure of nested SLE$_{6}$ loops via quantum disk fusion. This approach allows us to derive the joint distribution of nested regions bounded by these loops, and we also establish the conformal map law for the upper boundary of the region between two counter-clockwise oriented loops, describing its structure in terms of quantum disks and sphere pockets.

The NBIC working group, which is part of a broader initiative, is working to standardize the normalization of quantitative image biomarkers, ensuring their portability across different platforms and applications. By organizing working groups that address specific issues, the NBIC is working to develop consistent methodologies for image and biomarker data management and analysis. A recent publication outlines the initial efforts of the NBIC in identifying key issues and working towards image and image marker normalization. The long-term goal of the NBIC is to promote the portability of image-based biomarkers and data across different research initiatives and software implementations.

We examine the high-spin nucleon and delta excitations in the process of $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction using the $SU(3)$ relativistic quark model. Initially, we establish spatial and spin-flavor wave functions for baryons in terms of quark fields and determine their mass and wave function parameters through the delta excitation in the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction off the nucleon. Then, we establish spatial and spin-flavor wave functions for the high-spin nucleon and include it to describe the delta excitation reaction. Our model successfully replicates experimental data, including recent results from J-PARC, and indicates notable high-spin nucleon and delta excitation contributions. Specifically, we find that the high-spin nucleon excitation manifests in both the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ final states, whereas the delta excitation is predominantly present in the $K\Sigma$ final state.

This research introduces a set of techniques to prepare images from the database for subsequent processing, aligning with the principles of the Histogram of Morphotropic Local Binary Patterns (HBiMLBP) descriptor used in facial recognition. It details the implementation of the proposed method and its application to images from the MORPH-II face collection, aiming to enhance recognition accuracy through the application of enhanced descriptors on pre-processed facial images. Non-Uniform Sampling, a principle of enhanced descriptors, necessitates the evaluation of the approach's effectiveness on database images. Visualizations are provided to illustrate the techniques employed for image preparation.

When the curvaton field is included in the standard cosmological model, its dynamics cause the effective spacetime curvature to increase, leading to the formation of a primordial black hole with a specific mass related to the Planck mass. This process, in which the curvaton roll drives black hole creation, can be simplified in the stiff matter dominated phase and is analyzed in detail in this study.

Recent advancements in educational analytics have highlighted underrepresented research areas such as curriculum design, which can be effectively enhanced by statistical latent variable models and network analysis techniques. We develop an innovative approach combining these methodologies to provide a more comprehensive understanding of students' educational experiences and pathways. By tracking multiple dimensions of student activity across their academic journey, this approach generates implicit interest indicators and allows for a detailed exploration of how these interests evolve over time. We demonstrate the utility of this method using synthetic data and apply it to the Harvard University course completion data from 1900-2019, providing insights into both student and institutional-level changes in interests.

A novel autonomous control strategy for vehicle platoons is presented, allowing dynamic adjustment of inter-vehicle spacing based on on-board camera feeds. By treating each vehicle as a game player, this approach allows it to optimally respond to the control actions of other vehicles in its immediate vicinity, thereby minimizing the impact of external disturbances and uncooperative vehicles. To address potential conflicts in control, a comprehensive set of constraints is imposed, guaranteeing smooth and seamless integration of each vehicle's actions. To efficiently solve the complex optimization problem generated by this approach, a data-driven method using positive definite functions is employed. This method enables the determination of optimal control policies and their implementation via a software processor on each on-board computer. Simulations have demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach, revealing its capacity to handle unexpected disturbances and uncooperative vehicles while maintaining smooth and efficient traffic flow.

The relationship between an explanatory variable and the logistic regression's bias term can be critical, with the possibility of severe issues like interaction occurring if not carefully managed, where estimates become unreliable, highly variable, and difficult to interpret. We examined the relationship between adjustable terms, the bias, and the overall estimated model, and developed techniques to eliminate interaction within specific ranges of the explanatory variable, as well as automated filtering to identify areas of influence and set corresponding bias constraints for each discovered region, making previously set constraints redundant, and ultimately leading to simplified, non-decreasing models with few parameters, and we established that the adjusted linear bias term has superior statistical properties, including minimal variance, compared to its unadjusted counterpart, and provided an adjusted version of the F-test for assessing the significance of adjustable terms. Our findings are validated through simulations and real-world data analysis.

The rise in 3D printing technology enables the creation of intricate objects previously impossible to manufacture, including headline-shaped objects.
Headlines are desirable due to their realistic depth perception and the ability to convey precise metric information.
However, their high complexity and existing production limitations restrict their widespread use.
To optimize the production of headlines, it is essential to distinguish between those created using 3D printing and those made using traditional techniques.
We introduce DefNet, a definition-based model, which identifies 3D-printed objects by learning the semantic differences between mechanically and non-mechanically created items.
DefNet incorporates the definition of a object and uses a transformer-based architecture, incorporating an attention mechanism to process the object's features.
We evaluate DefNet's effectiveness on synthetic and real datasets. Our model outperforms baseline methods, with a significant improvement in classification accuracy on synthetic data.
Moreover, DefNet effectively improves the classification performance on real datasets, with a substantial increase in accuracy from 64% to 79%.

In polycrystalline and amorphous materials, conventional magnetic order is often prevented due to extensive local strains. We examine a spin triplet fermionic system in a spinless background as a model for charge-2k anyons and find that polycrystalline and amorphous arrangements can give rise to a stable chiral spin liquid state. This outcome is driven by the Nagaev interaction between spin triplet anyons, which also supports a possible link between topological order in chiral spin liquids and these polycrystalline/amorphous frameworks. We also show that introducing weak exchange interactions between neighbors can produce a dynamic anyon-lattice gas behavior near the chiral spin liquid state.

The key to building large-scale radio telescopes lies in precise measurements of station positions. Current methods for determining these measurements involve using long baseline optical interferometers known as calibration facilities. These can measure the lengths of interferometric paths between various station pairs with sub-millimeter accuracy. To effectively use data collected by these calibration facilities, a complex mathematical approach is necessary, involving the calculation of distances between all stations and subsequent, computationally demanding operations. Current processing methods have a significant drawback, with computation and storage requirements increasing quadratically as the number of stations grows. To address this issue, we've developed new algorithms that maintain a and and log n scaling, respectively. Our methods make efficient use of data collected by calibration facilities, allowing for improved telescope calibration.

Recent advancements in deep generative adversarial networks have led to innovative applications in financial fields such as risk measurement, portfolio optimization, and forecasting. A novel variant of conditional GAN, known as autoencoding conditional GAN, is capable of accurately reproducing complex real-world data distributions, including financial data. Our contribution lies in utilizing this AE-CGAN variant, specifically tailored to return series data, where inputs consist of relevant economic indicators. Through ablation studies, AECGAN exhibits superior performance compared to traditional methods, yielding lower prediction errors and higher forecast power relative to the S&P500 index. Furthermore, our research demonstrates how incorporating multiple GAN-generated samples into mean-CVaR portfolio optimization can lead to enhanced real-world portfolio performance.

The gluon-to-parton splitting functions play a key role in the DGLAP equations governing parton distribution functions within hadrons. These splitting functions, denoted by $P_{ij}(z, N)$, dictate how a parton transforms into another, where for instance, $P_{gg}(N)$ governs gluon splitting into additional gluons, $P_{gq}(N)$ describes gluon splitting into quarks, and $P_{gT}(N)$ represents the gluon top PDF. Research on these functions using asymptotic freedom in QCD has significantly advanced our understanding, particularly at $O(\alpha_s^3)$ for $P_{gq}(N)$. Our study comprehensively summarizes the $O(\alpha_s^3)$ calculation of $A_{gq}(N)$, detailing each step and employing the massive fermion scheme for accuracy, using the Hilbert's function to streamline calculations.

A new approach utilizing Bayesian artificial networks is presented for classifying and analyzing the energy spectra of Blazars provided by Fermi-LAT. The results indicate a connection between the NLBA classification accuracy and the radio properties of Blazars. Furthermore, the study reveals that a network configuration is capable of distinguishing between sources with and without Data-bins exceeding 10 GeV in their energy spectra, and another network can accurately classify sources containing both Data-bins above 10 GeV and LAXAGepeaks below 10 GeV. The research also provides an exploration of the NLBA classifications in relation to the radio properties of Blazars and an analysis of the link between LAXAGepeaks below 10 GeV and Blazar subtypes, and finally outlines the benefits and limitations of this research compared to a conventional machine learning approach using 22 parameters.

The rise of synthetic data has drawn interest, particularly in social media content.
However, a challenge arises when it comes to determining the maximum achievable
frequency of a particular piece of content. To address this, the paper "A Frequency
Limit on Social Media: Analysis and Applications" proposes a framework for finding
the maximum attainable frequency of a specific post. The study begins with a basic
model capturing key features of social media sharing behavior, and its findings are
corroborated with actual data collected from Facebook. Analysis shows that post
popularity is closely linked to the number of shares and that high-ranking pages
tend to be shared more widely, and that initial sharing rates are predictive of
ultimate popularity. Additionally, the model is applied to identify potential
maximum post frequencies on social media.

In this paper, we define and examine the concept of tensor product of hypergraphs, followed by exploring the connections between their spectra and combinatorial properties. By generating specific examples, we demonstrate the application of our findings. Furthermore, we prove that for certain given parameters, there exist paired hypergraphs whose combinatorial structures produce identical common image set sizes under tensor product.

Insist the Indian Space Research Organisation is set to launch in 2031.
This cutting-edge space telescope will revolutionize our understanding of the universe by studying distant galaxies and quasar populations across a vast range of cosmic time, as well as observing star formation in the present day.
To achieve its goals, Insist will utilize advanced technology to capture detailed images and data across multiple wavelengths, including the near-infrared and optical spectrum.
These capabilities will allow scientists to investigate the complex relationships between dark energy, galaxy evolution, and the birth of stars over an extended period of cosmic history.
Insist will conduct an in-depth analysis of the properties of dark energy by studying the luminosity and shape of standard candles located at significant redshifts, as well as the evolution of galaxies at redshifts exceeding 6.
By comparing observed galaxy properties with those expected from model predictions, researchers will gain new insights into the processes of galaxy evolution, star formation, and reionization.
Insist will also perform an extensive investigation of the origin and evolution of supermassive black holes in the early universe, as well as the interplay between active galactic nuclei and their surrounding environments, at redshifts exceeding 4.
By comparing the colors and brightness of active galactic nuclei with those of their host galaxies, researchers will gain a deeper understanding of the relationships between these phenomena, as well as the nature of the intergalactic medium at redshifts exceeding 6

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's, various outcomes like cognitive function and disease progression are often evaluated. Standard metrics, however, may not capture complex changes and might not be suitable for this diseased population. A more comprehensive approach, like using longitudinal curves, can provide a detailed understanding but comes with increased statistical complexity. To address this complexity and facilitate straightforward inference, researchers developed novel methods to analyze modified primary endpoints in clinical trials with multiple, continuous outcomes and correlated outcomes. By analyzing data from two Alzheimer's disease trials, one using the PACC score and the other using SPECT data, researchers demonstrated that their increased primary endpoint can detect more subtle effects and increase statistical power compared to standard metrics, all while maintaining comparable type I error rates.

In path-based approaches, methods like instantons and shoelaces have been used to find dominant pathways between complex systems' free energy minima. To generalize these approaches, we developed an algorithm that globally optimizes the action, based on molecular dynamics simulations, to discover pathways between minima. This algorithm relies on a generative model to define pathway shapes and was applied to locate transition pathways in two undercooled liquid models, successfully capturing key features and mechanisms like plastic crystal nucleation and reentrant freezing. By tuning the model, we modeled diverse nucleation mechanisms and found the boundaries between different pathways. This method offers a new way to investigate complex transitions, allowing us to explore the space of pathways and identify a wide range of transition pathways, including those that may coexist with observed pathways or exist at comparable free energy levels.

This paper focuses on solving the complex Monge-Ampere and Hessian equations within a parabolic framework. A key objective of the study involves establishing the presence of L^∞ evaluation for smooth solutions to the given parabolic equations with specified boundary conditions. Furthermore, we aim to provide an detailed analysis of L^∞ evaluation in low regularity settings for these parabolic equations.

We've developed a 'typed context lambda-calculus with a finite variation operator, which has strong connections to a specific category of regular functions. This operator allows the lambda-calculus to be closed, which in turn facilitates a corresponding, efficient term size evaluation. Furthermore, by incorporating several type constructors, including natural numbers, finite and infinite products, and universal and existential quantifiers, the lambda-calculus becomes a powerful tool for computation. Notably, this lambda-calculus has been demonstrated to exactly replicate a vast array of previously established computational lambda-calculi, effectively representing numerous well-established functions and mathematical proofs within its framework, without incurring excessive term size inflation.

This study examines stochastic differential equations of Stratonovich and Ito types, which involve random processes with state probability density as their integrands. It's observed that these equations can be seen as a special case of a generalized mean theorem, applicable to Stratonovich integrals, and also yields a novel representation of the state probability density in an Einstein-Smoluchowski diffusion equation in terms of the conditional probability density of a Brownian motion.

Building on previous research, specifically a 2015 paper, this work develops a comprehensive framework to study cohomology and concepts such as uniform boundedness and polynomial growth in the context of group actions on standard spaces. This framework has a broader application, extending to a broader class of group actions on tree-like spaces introduced by Bestvine and Brumfiel, with an in-depth examination included in a separate paper.

This paper presents a comprehensive linguistic model for text-to-SQL tasks, focusing on cross-domain applicability. The proposed framework consists of two key components: a text encoding module and a SQL generation module, both designed to include an auxiliary task that enhances SQL accuracy.
