This paper presents an approach to estimate Kendall's tau, measuring the correlation between two variables, by leveraging precise effect sizes from their binary interactions. A simple naive method yields biased results, so a solution is developed to resolve and reduce this bias. Our method initially calculates the natural correlation between the variables and then transforms it into Kendall's tau using a semiparametric model based on score functions and Edgeworth expansions. This solution maintains high accuracy, exhibiting minimal error with an average of $.5 \times 10^{-5}$ on multiple datasets, exceeding the current standard of CRANK. Additionally, the technique can be integrated into Bayesian models through data augmentation and demonstrates faster convergence in MCMC processes.

Integrating edge intelligence, AI, and IoT in vehicular networks enables novel applications, including safety alerts, navigation assistance, and edge cloud services, but raises concerns about user privacy due to extensive vehicle data collection. To address this challenge, a comprehensive framework has been developed to safeguard user privacy through differential privacy mechanisms, allowing a flexible selection and combination of differential privacy strategies. By employing a dynamic budget allocation framework, multiple vehicle users can receive varying levels of privacy protection, whereas the system preserves its overall privacy protection budget. To further expand the available privacy protection budget, a proposed trading mechanism enables the exchange of unneeded privacy protection between system and individual users. The framework's performance has been evaluated through comprehensive simulations, showcasing its versatility and adaptability.

This article begins by defining the Euler Topology surface using properties from algebraic topology, specifically the characteristics of graphs, surfaces, and polyhedra. It then explores the properties of Euler surfaces and examines how graphs, polyhedra, and polyhedra with a specific structure called caged behave within the framework of Euler surfaces.

This article explores the long-term behavior and stability of a modified Holling-Tanner predator-prey model with an increased strong Allee effect in the prey population. As a result, the model expands to three dimensions, and we demonstrate through mathematical derivation that all trajectories within its domain converge to stable equilibrium points, including two unstable centers, two unstable planes, and two stable surfaces, as well as two stable states with complete predator extinction. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the stable equilibrium points are fundamentally either two-dimensional planes or three-dimensional surfaces, indicating a holistic and collective extinction event for the species involved, or total coexistence.

Our previous investigation successfully applied the aspect pivot technique to solve nonlinear programming in the multivariate case by constraining the objective function with linear equations. This current study further develops the approach, now allowing a single, non-linear objective function without any linear constraints. The study proves a crucial hypothesis: at each iteration, the feasible region's diameter diminishes proportionally, provided certain conditions are met regarding matrix and vector norms.

This paper explores how gauge theory principles can be used to reduce uncertainties when extracting the top quark mass from $ttj$ events at the LHC. These events are subject to substantial corrections from non-factorizable effects, which influence the off-shell top quark distribution. These corrections arise due to final-state radiation (FSR) effects on the leptonic decay width of a top quark. Our findings suggest that a simple method for accounting for off-shell effects on the differential cross-section of $ttj$ occurrences can be used, and these effects are negligible at the central values of the analysis cuts used in an ATLAS-tau-t analysis for the top quark mass extraction. Consequently, these effects can be treated as part of the overall systematic uncertainty without significantly impacting the result.

Deepfakes have become a pressing concern in recent years, posing significant challenges for security. Specifically, research has focused on the difficulty of detecting AI-generated faces within the OSNI class of deepfakes. This study investigates the efficiency of self-attention networks in learning zero-shot classification within deepfake detection, using the OSNI category. By incorporating feature extraction networks trained on large datasets, this work evaluates multiple vision transformer architectures, comparing them to established vision transformer and CNN baselines in real-world deepfake detection settings. Experiments conducted on the largest deepfake benchmark, Celeb-DF, reveal a substantial performance advantage for self-attention networks, with light-weight configurations significantly narrowing the gap with CNN baselines, despite limited model capacity. This breakthrough enables deepfakes to be detected with a remarkable 90% accuracy using lightweight models. The accompanying code and models can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/alexgusev/Deepfake-Detection-ViT.

The objective of this project involves the implementation of a Neural Network-based
automated driving model using simulated data. In this simulated environment, multiple
scenarios are available and a Neural Network is trained to navigate vehicles through them.
Once trained, the model is adapted for real-world application. Initially, the project relied
on basic features, but was upgraded to incorporate features relevant to actual driving.
A key limitation of this work lies in the absence of traffic signal consideration.

In real-world applications, Multi-objective Evolutionary Algorithms (MOEAs) are often constrained by time, leading to asynchronous parallel arrangements where an algorithm terminates within a set timeframe. Prior studies, led by those on the AnsA benchmark for comparing time-bounded MOEAs, overlooked one crucial factor - runtime behavior, failing to do so in a comprehensive manner. Asynchronous parallel setups lead to a certain selection mechanism that can cause a bias in the evolution process due to their inherent latency issues influencing individual run times. Consequently, faster individuals are more likely to be selected. To tackle this problem, we introduce a new parent selection mechanism based on frequency rather than fitness, aiming to mitigate the bias. Experimental findings demonstrate that frequency-based selection reduces the bias's impact and outperforms existing schemes. Furthermore, integrating frequency-based selection with traditional fitness-based selection yields a hybrid strategy that strikes a balance and achieves superior results over existing practices on AnsA.

The exoplanet system, near the Milky Way's center, has been discovered to contain a large cold world, with an estimated mass of 6.2 Jupiter masses, located about 4.25 arcminutes from the center. Discovered using a microlensing technique, its exact nature was confirmed with the Keck telescope's near-infrared imaging and spectroscopy. The world, with an estimated age of 9 billion years, has a temperature of around 35 Kelvin and a radius of around 2.2 Earth radii, density calculations suggest a rocky body with a thick atmosphere. Detailed analysis further verified the a priori parameters of the system, indicating a semi-major axis of around 3.2 AU and an eccentricity of around 0.25. Further research with the Keck telescope and a model of a nitrogen-rich atmosphere revealed a high pressure of around 200 bar and significant methane absorption, although no water vapor absorption was detected. The atmosphere's composition and properties were discussed in detail and compared to other known exoplanets and brown dwarfs, and further research is suggested to further verify the system's properties.

A general mathematical framework has been established to expand time-dependent Markovian dynamics in a rapid time-oscillation parameter, allowing for the derivation of effective evolution generators. These generators can be calculated order by order and often comprise discrete quantum control in a rapid time field. The approach is versatile and versatile, applicable to both non-Markovian and MKOV dynamics, homogeneous and inhomogeneous states, and complex multi-level systems. The method was verified through rigorous checks and was demonstrated in various areas of physics. The expansion was initially developed to investigate adiabatic invariants in quantum open systems, but it has since been applied to a wide range of problems, such as a two-level system in a rapidly changing electromagnetic field, the spin-1/2 Pauli blocking problem, and a generalized quantum blocking problem.

Neutron inelastic scattering was used to study the effect of solid solution with rhodium on the crystal structure, magnetic properties, and phase transitions in CePd. We found that small changes in rhodium composition led to significant impacts on the neutron depolarization profile. Notably, compositions near x = 0.2 and x = 0.6 exhibited depolarization related to magnetic transitions and possible magnetic order, with x = 0.6 showing signs of antiferromagnetic order. As rhodium was added to CePd, its ability to order ferromagnetically decreased, but its transition temperature increased, indicating that the role of free magnetic moments was altered. These findings highlight the intricate interplay between the electronic structure and magnetic order in these materials, specifically the competition between antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic tendencies and how it influences the electronic state.

A comprehensive investigation of 32 high-velocity HI self-absorption events has been conducted, which were discovered in a detailed survey of the region G176.51+00.20. The study aims to understand these events' implications for the dynamics and interplay between the large-scale molecular and HI clouds. It includes an examination of the region's molecular and HI kinematics, as well as its interaction with the surrounding interstellar medium. HI self-absorptions exhibit a wide range of properties such as velocities, velocities differences, foreground-contour, and column density, which can be categorized into four distinct groups based on these characteristics. The observed HI self-absorptions involving large negative velocity differences are believed to be associated with the large molecular complex surrounding G176.51+00.20, which is likely undergoing significant interaction with the surrounding HI interstellar medium, resulting in the formation of HI self-absorptions. Furthermore, the investigation of the HI self-absorptions involving small negative velocity differences reveals the presence of interplay between molecular clouds and HI.

The concept of base $\beta$ expansions can be expanded to irrational $\beta$ > 1, resulting in expansions with gaps or holes where no numbers have a finite expansion. The set of numbers with no such gaps, known as the set $X_\beta$, has a specific $\beta$-critical value, but a more general case exists. This broader condition requires that sequences leading to gaps can be avoided after some point, and it is within this general case that we focus on a more specific scenario. Here, we focus on avaricious $\beta$-numbers, a subset of the general condition where all sequences leading to gaps can be avoided immediately, and we show that this specific scenario contains a previously identified subset known as the avaricious $\beta$-numbers with a gap.

Researchers have made a groundbreaking discovery by measuring for the first time a CP-violating angle in certain particle transformations. The study involved analyzing data from nearly 19 million Bs meson decays into two pi mesons, utilizing the LHCb experiment's superior ability to isolate specific particle trajectories, particularly in the u-variant environment offered by the s-sbar condensed state. Analysis in the S-matrix formalism confirmed a non-zero value for sin φs of approximately 0.10 with a statistical significance of 4.1σ, aligning with theoretical expectations and showing consistency with a previously estimated φs value from other decay patterns.

This study introduces a novel evaluation method for determining the scope and boundaries of deep neural network domain transfer when applying a network trained on one dataset to a different testing dataset. The proposed approach is empirically validated through analysis of results obtained from training a neural network on the CIFAR-10 dataset and evaluating its performance under normal circumstances and adversarial attacks. Our experiments, conducted using both adversarial examples and random noise, demonstrate the network's capability to accurately classify images from nearby manifolds while experiencing noticeable drops in accuracy for images from more distant distributions. The results demonstrate that this method effectively identifies the point at which the network's accuracy falls below a specified threshold for different testing distributions, thereby delineating its domain transfer limits. The experiments also highlight the network's ability to transition from a nearby testing distribution to a common vision dataset and then to an entirely different image classification dataset, thus illustrating the successful extension of its application beyond the original training domain.

In this note, for any finite field, we calculate the average number of arc connections between two points on the field's points. Additionally, for specific finite fields $\mathbb F_q$, where $q$ is even, we calculate the expected arc connection count precisely. Our approach relies on a crucial lemma that can be applied to determine arc connection counts within various subsets of $\mathbb F_q^2$.

This paper explores a physical method for visually representing mathematical proof through an experimental arrangement that yet alone conveys its concept. The concept is exemplified by demonstrating the area of a polygon's decomposition into its constituent parts. The choice of decomposition into equilateral triangles rather than the conventional triangular ones, stems from the ease with which the latter can be created in a physical setting.

Deep Graph Neural Networks demonstrate exceptional performance, yet they face significant challenges in debugging, optimizing, and generalizing due to their complex structure. This paper introduces the Parameterized Interpreter to address these issues, allowing for the customizable evaluation of specific GNN architectures with adjustable parameters and evaluators. By generalizing common GNN networks like GCN and GAT and introducing a novel GNN architecture called PAGNN, the Parameterized Interpreter givess researchers the ability to explore novel designs and easily compare them to existing approaches. Experiments on multiple datasets confirm the Parameterized Interpreter's capability in achieving high performance and generalization, particularly with the PAGNN architecture.

The peculiar system RXCJ0232.2+4420, observed in a detailed examination, displays an unusual distribution of its hot gas, where the southern half exhibits higher X-ray brightness compared to the northern half. The cluster's gas appears highly magnetized and rotating. Notably, the sharp, dense boundary between the southern and northern halves, known as a shock front, shows no signs of recent substructure collisions. However, the team found evidence of a candidate substructure in the southern half, characterized by lower temperature and magnetic properties than its surroundings. The temperature in this area, along with its surrounding medium, shows a steady decline along the cluster's rotation axis, giving rise to a hypothesis that the substructure could be the result of the southern half undergoing a slow-down rotation. The team's proposed model, where the system formed through the merger of two previously relaxed systems, is less favored, given its symmetry. The researchers suggest an alternative explanation, where the system formed through the merger of the southern half and a previously relaxed structure from the east.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Module (LMM), a type of state-space model, has emerged
as a top-performing approach in handling time-series data, especially on benchmark
datasets like split-UCR-UCR. To further enhance LMM's capabilities and scale it for
varied dataset sizes, a memory-efficient and fast training strategy is necessary. MemoryEF
is designed for this purpose, and it demonstrates the ability to process memory in linear
time in relation to the dataset's size. MemoryEF achieves this efficiency by optimizing
the memory of the LMM and reordering data sequences for training, specifically using
a method called MemoryEF-reorder. Our research shows that MemoryEF maintains training
effectiveness, matching model accuracy with data sequence length of approximately one-fifth
to one-tenth the original. These results highlight the feasibility of scaling LMM through data
size reduction, making it an effective and flexible approach for training neural networks.

This review paper outlines the findings from direct particle collision experiments and the most recent developments in theory that have led to the search for cosmic contributors to dark matter and nucleon constituents that have an extremely low interaction rate. Specifically, the low interaction properties that these new particles exhibit with standard model particles are quantified and how this knowledge is applied to the design of highly sensitive detection experiments are described in detail. The interaction strength is demonstrated to be comparable to either a single particle force or a more complex many-particle effect, resulting in observable effects that range from the formation of bound states to the scattering of particles. A thorough description of the current experimental status, future research directions, and theoretical models of new physics beyond the standard model are also included.

We are working towards achieving linguistic consistency within the Ising model by introducing a new game theory framework. In this game, spins are represented by two distinct players - Alice and Bob. Although they have opposing initial strategies, they share a common objective. Each spin flips to improve its spin energy, which corresponds to a player's payoff in the game. Consistency is reached when Alice and Bob have the same pure and mixed strategy preferences. We focus on a scenario where players can migrate between sites and determine the conditions for consistency in this context.

Deep learning has achieved notable advancements in solving inverse problems governed by partial differential equations (PDDs). Nonetheless, these discoveries are often hindered by the bias inherent in neural networks regarding spectral properties, a crucial aspect to consider when formulating problems from PDEs. Investigating the impact of this spectral bias through ablation studies, this study demonstrates that the inclusion of momentum in stochastic gradient descent can mitigate the consequences of this bias, yielding faster convergence and improved accuracy when approximating problems with high-frequency high-dimensional characteristics, whereas the benefits are less pronounced when dealing with issues that are not spectrally biased. Additionally, the study finds that the choice of network architecture and the type of noise present do not significantly influence the spectrum of a problem, whereas the type of data sampler and spatial noise do. Furthermore, the research finds that the benefits of using momentum are not due to increased optimizer stability, suggesting that the mechanism by which momentum overcomes the limitations of these neural networks is an area of further investigation.

This study builds upon a prior associated paper by analyzing one-dimensional linked wave systems featuring variable damping of the Kelvin-Voigt type. Notably, it achieves full exponential stability without imposing the one-dimensional Hirshberg condition on these systems. This stability is further confirmed to be independent in nature. We establish that exponentially stable subcategories exist within the broader framework of considered systems. This can be conceptualized as follows: (a) we demonstrate that any specified subset of the 1D linked system class can be embedded within a 1D system featuring periodically variable damping. Consequently, a priori analysis of the perturbed systems developed in the linked waves paper is applicable to this embedded class. This results in subcategories of the embedded class which are both fully exponentially stable without imposing the Hirshberg condition and independent. Subcategories of locally perturbed systems are shown to share these same qualities.

Model-based reinforcement learning approaches seek to explicitly learn a representation of the environment from which optimal policies can be derived. In contrast, most model-free reinforcement learning techniques rely on implicit learning of value functions and policies without providing any explanation of their behavior. In real-world applications, there is often a need to not only understand the environment but also to explain the learned policies in a way that is easily interpretable. In hierarchical reinforcement learning, optimal policies at the higher level can be modeled as projections of the environment states onto subsets of possible goals, making it feasible to explain them as logic programs. However, typically there is no straightforward connection between these projections and the behaviors learned at the lower policy level, resulting in a lack of justification for the predicted projections. 

To address this issue, we propose a model-based reinforcement learning approach that involves learning an interpretable world model using logical reasoning. By learning logical fluents that correspond to various goals and explaining them using inductive logic programming, we can establish a link between the learned projections and the behaviors learned at the lower policy level, thus making the entire process more transparent and justifiable.

We've shown that in a three-level atom system, exciting nonresonant photons can prevent reversed absorption by inducing a coherence effect between resonant photons. This phenomenon showcases the intricate connections between high-frequency photons at nonresonant frequencies and low-frequency resonant photons, potentially enabling control over light propagation through and detection of nonresonant frequencies.

We develop a novel approach inspired by Fenton's work on a related concept. Specifically, we use a stochastic process defined over a finite space of signals to create a measure of a function, denoted $\mathcal{F}$, given its values at randomly sampled points. This method can be applied to any space of signals. We compare this approach to a deterministic solution, optimizing the same objective function at the same sample points. By controlling the variance of the sampling distribution, our method provides a way to bound the difference between the stochastic and deterministic solutions. This decision-theoretic framework allows us to generalize existing results and reveals connections between neural network training via minimax and its alternative using random features. We further illustrate these connections by applying our framework to specific spaces of signals, namely a bandlimited and a finite dimensional one.

The behavior of scintillation light in DCASET$^1$ detectors is analyzed in relation to the dynamics of dark matter-nucleon interactions. Specifically, the study focuses on the dynamic form factors of $^6$Li, utilizing a shell-model analysis to examine low-energy transitions. To better understand the spin-dependent interaction of $^6$Li, the study presents calculations of matrix elements of the $^6$Li asymmetry operator, which are utilized in an exam of DCASET's detection capabilities. DCASET's inherent ability to separate electronic and nuclear recoils is used to set the most current bounds on the dark matter-nucleon interaction cross-section for DM masses below 10 MeV, surpassing previous experiments on scintillation light in DT targets and targeting the upper end of the parameter space predicted by leading WIMP candidates.

A groundbreaking approach to single-image restoration has emerged as a leading strategy in the field. Nevertheless, the success of this method is heavily dependent on the quality and scope of the paired training data available. Acquiring comprehensive paired datasets, which include images with diverse degradations and degradations-free counterparts, poses significant challenges in practice. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel blind image restoration technique grounded in the concept of a kernel mixture. This method formulates the image restoration problem as a sequence of Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) decompositions in the pixel, gradient, and Laplacian domains. By leveraging the benefits of the kernelization process, the proposed method effectively models complex data patterns with simpler parameters, making it suitable for tasks such as image denoising, deconvolution, and deraining. Through its innovative use of a multi-domain GMM decomposition, the proposed method achieves enhanced restoration capabilities with minimal trainable parameters. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the superiority of the method in the context of single-image restoration. The accompanying source code is available for public use.

This article introduces and examines two novel formulations of nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equations, which depend on a pair of subspaces within a Lie algebra. A particular case arises when the subspaces comprise a complementary pair. These equations have a significant relation to a dual problem involving R-matrix-based representations and co-coal based co-representations. Moreover, we demonstrate that the nonuniform Yang-Baxter equation ensures the b-coalgebra axioms are met in a particular twisted setting, which in turn allows the construction of infinite families of solutions through the use of representation and co-representation pairs.

The discovery of Hoare logic marked a turning point in the formal verification of software, as it introduced a pioneering approach to formally specifying and proving the correctness of software. Building upon Hoare's foundational work, researchers have been developing more precise and conceptually intuitive frameworks, aiming to simplify logical expressions, increase their expressiveness, and enhance applicability. This study introduces a new framework for software validation called Natural Hoare Logic (NHL), which seeks to bridge the gap between traditional software specifications and code by integrating statements from everyday language into the verification process. Our work also sheds light on a critical challenge in software verification: translating between linguistic expressions and logical formulas, which is a key factor in achieving greater practical relevance. We also detail a formal semantics for software validation using a mathematical method called modal translation, as well as establish the equivalence between this semantics and the traditional Hoare triples. Furthermore, we outline a proof system for validations, which relies on existing Hoare logic axioms, rules, and the principles of modal logic.

Consensus algorithms, like Canopus, are designed to ensure various forms of failure and eventual agreement among agents in complex networks with different types of failures, from isolated failures to coordinated attacks by malicious agents. However, the original Canopus protocol assumes that agents always successfully complete their internal computations, leading to performance issues when agents fail to finish due to resource constraints caused by failures. Additionally, it doesn't take into account cases where agents are controlled by malicious agents who intentionally try to disrupt the computation. To overcome these limitations, we present RCanopus, a modified version of Canopus, that can handle failures and coordinated attacks by masking failed computations and filtering out malicious agents' messages, allowing the system to reach a consensus despite failures and increases in the number of agents and their behaviors. Our analysis shows that RCanopus leads to a rapid agreement among agents and maintains its stability even during failures, while our simulation demonstrates its efficiency compared to Canopus, completing each round of work in less time.

Our research involves investigating the elasticity of lipid membranes containing cholesterol via atomistic molecular dynamics simulations. By examining the fluctuations in these membranes, we calculate their elasticity and compare results for three distinct lipid types. Notably, our findings reveal a modest increase in elasticity for the lightest lipid type when 20% cholesterol is present, but this trend diminishes for the other lipids studied.

By integrating the constraints from the ADM Hamiltonian and diffeomorphism into the loop quantum mechanical framework, we develop a quantum version of loop quantum gravity. This enables us to create a local model for testing the effects of noncommutative space on atomic spectra, specifically on hydrogen-like atoms. To achieve this, we derive a quantum version of the Schrödinger equation and solve it for lowest-lying states. Our initial calculations include calculating expectation values of kinetic and potential energy and determining energy levels. These results can be compared with results from noncommutative field theoretical approaches, while also providing guidance for potential experimental testing.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog presents an updated list of 34 highest-energy cosmic rays with energies exceeding 5.76 × 10¹⁹ eV, based on analyses from the first six years of its operation. This catalog reveals several intriguing patterns when examining directions of extensive air showers in pairs. Notably, two pairs of events are documented with apparent large angular separations, yet with energies and arrival directions that suggest a possible correlation. This catalog will be officially released to the public upon the publication of a comprehensive multivariate search result.

This study introduces BayesOD, a novel Bayesian approach for quantifying the uncertainty in object detection output from Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Unlike traditional methods, BayesOD accurately captures uncertainty across different types of errors, including confusions between objects, localized errors, and random detection outliers. Utilizing an objective information theoretic metric, the method accurately measures uncertainty without being overly cautious. Our results confirm that BayesOD effectively calibrates uncertainty and its components without requiring any object localization information, making it highly versatile. Furthermore, we demonstrate that combining detected objects from multiple DNNs, based on uncertainty, significantly enhances detector precision. Our method's effectiveness is confirmed through experiments on various object detection datasets, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet, KITTI, and Kuznetrkotk, and its open-source implementation is available on GitHub.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive review of traffic prediction models, focusing particularly on the perspective of traffic representation rather than the prediction aspect. Traffic representation involves encoding traffic patterns as traffic moving segments (TMS), which reveal distinct characteristics such as smooth segment, ramp merge, ramp diverge, choke point, bottleneck, and chocked, among others. Among the identified TMS types, choke points, bottlenecks, and chocked points are classified as critical segments, while others are categorized as non-critical. Existing research predominantly relies on scalar traffic prediction techniques, often neglecting precise traffic representation and the in-depth understanding of TMS. Given that the shape and duration of TMS significantly influence traffic representation accuracy, the proposed framework aims to integrate traffic representation learning into a unified framework capable of producing both scalar and TMS predictions simultaneously. Furthermore., we aim to develop a novel classification system to identify the type of TMS, ultimately enabling the prediction of both continuous values and discrete labels using probabilistic approaches, based on the model's prediction of probability distributions.

We develop a rewriting system in the Gray class class with a focus on its multi-step format. A specific sub-class within the Gray class class, characterized by a maximal step length, allows for a top-level element to be identified, which in turn enables the definition of concurrency. This top-level element's existence is proven under certain conditions, namely when a level-preserving reduction system is applied. These conditions are further illustrated through examples, which involve the rewriting systems for the process algebras ACPN, iACP, and the extended process algebra BPA(A). Our work primarily revolves around the concept of consistency within the process algeras, which we analyze under the bisimulation.

Automated hippocampal segmentation in neuroimaging is a time-consuming and error-prone process, particularly for patients with neurological disorders, particularly those with epilepsy. Hippocampal shape and volume, key indicators in diagnosing epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease, pose a particular challenge due to the severe shape distortations caused by epilepsy. Existing hippocampal automatic segmentation tools, designed for healthy individuals, struggle when applied to epilepsy cases, often resulting in misclassification and incorrect diagnoses. To address this issue, this study presents a multi-branch deep learning network, which partitions the hippocampus into sub-regions in cases of epilepsy and neurodegenerative disorders. Each branch processes distinct hippocampal regions and employs shape constraints to ensure accurate sub-regional boundaries. Validation through quantitative assessment demonstrates significantly improved regional accuracy in epilepsy cases compared to state-of-the-art segmentation methods.

We propose and experimentally evaluate the semi-definite transversal mode of emission from single photons. Our findings confirm that this mode is inherently ambiguous and can be understood as a manifestation of the three-particle pigeonhole phenomenon. We further demonstrate its distinction from the two-mode polarization Bell-like state, highlighting its unique properties. By quantitatively comparing these two states, we reveal that the transversal mode encompasses the latter. Building on this insight, we devise an approach to experimentally verify the pertain relationship, utilizing a polarization measurement setup. Moreover, we establish a framework for expressing the density matrix of single photons in terms of transversal mode amplitudes. This amplitudes formula enables us to calculate key quantum optical parameters, including radial order, coherence width, and photon number distribution variance, revealing their inherent relationships. Our experimental results align with theoretical predictions, ultimately facilitating the resolution of practical applications involving single photons and spatial modes.

In recent years, researchers are increasingly focusing on Galactic Center Gamma Rays (CRAND) to investigate Galactic Center matter, but there have been limited studies on Cosmic Rays (CR) at Low Earth Orbits (LEO) captured by magnetic fields. A study using a LEO-mounted Monte Carlo simulation and comparing it to data from LEO-based instruments like CRRES and PAMELA, found that CR captured by magnetic fields at LEO exhibits distinct characteristics, including an elevated proton carbon-nucleus ratio and specific nuclear fragmentation products like He-3 and Li-7 that cannot be explained by standard models, suggesting that the simulation may be accurate in representing these unusual phenomena that could potentially result from the interaction of CR with dense Galactic Center matter captured by magnetic fields.

Deep Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) leverage graph neural networks and matrix spectral theory to achieve more efficient and theoretically grounded performance than other neural network architectures. However, spectral GNNs face challenges in achieving deep architectures due to a narrow and slow-shrinking pyramid in the eigenvalue distribution of Laplacian matrices, which severely restricts their representational capacity. To overcome these challenges, our work introduces a novel deep GNN framework, centered around a Shrinkage-Personalization framework. By integrating multi-scale pyramid-like shrinkage and local topology link reconfiguration techniques, our approach enhances the eigenvalue distribution to enable representational capacity expansion. Our numerical experiments confirm that this Shrinkage-Personalization framework effectively promotes the development of deep GNNs in terms of convergence efficiency and model performance compared to existing GNN architectures.

This study introduces the first differentially private solution for low-rank matrix matrix fulfillment problems, which encompass various real-world applications such as private matrix completion and machine learning. Similar to robust statistical estimation, the proposed approach utilizes the Huber loss function, providing theoretical assurances of privacy and accuracy. It presents two algorithms: an iterative method with theoretical privacy guarantees and a more efficient iterative alternative, which, although not theoretically privacy-assured, produces similar output accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed model and accompanying numerical analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of these algorithms, which outperform the standard nuclear norm regularization method.

We present a unified model for dust extinction, polarization, and emission in the interstellar medium by integrating an electron and proton component with a distribution of grains, starting from submicron-sized dust particles and extending to large, uniform grains. This comprehensive model accounts for grain growth and destruction processes in the sparse and dense interstellar medium through equilibrium grain size distributions composed of power-law and log-normal components for extinction and polarized scattering, and pure log-normal components for the emission of small, and and scattering of large grains. The model parameters are derived from astronomical observations of dust properties, and we provide a Python implementation called the Astronomical Dust Model with Dust Polarization (ADMDP), which generates the full 3D dust extinction, polarization, and emission spectra, as well as a simplified, low-computational-cost representation of polarized scattering and emission, which we termed the Polarized Element Representation (PER). Our results, based on an analysis of 777,600 points in the Milky Way, demonstrate a good agreement between our model predictions and the real-world data, particularly with respect to extinction and polarization data, and show reasonable consistency with the 777,600 points in the Milky Way, and the 777,600 points in the Milky Way.

A new discovery has challenged our understanding of brown dwarf binaries. Researchers found a massive brown dwarf, CIDA 1 B, orbiting close to a low-mass star, contradicting previous models. This is the first known brown dwarf to form within a protoplanetary disk rather than a circumstellar disk. The binary system, located in the Orion nebula, features CIDA 1 B with a mass of approximately 0.05 solar masses and a temperature of around 900 K. Spectroscopic analysis of CIDA 1 B reveals characteristics of T dwarfs, including methane and water absorption and thermal characteristics similar to field T4.5 dwarf objects. This unusual brown dwarf binary system presents a significant challenge to binary star formation theories.

In the game of Lights Out with an $m \times m$ grid, a maximum click point results from pressing the entire grid repeatedly. For a 2-dimensional grid, these points are characterized as those grid cells located at coordinates $(x,y)$ where either $x$ or $y$ is a multiple of $\gcd(2m, m-1)$. It's also demonstrated that for a 2-dimensional grid, there are multiple points that exhibit this behavior.

Image segmentation based on graph cuts has been widely used in image restoration, yet most image segmentation models do not consider the applications of image restoration techniques. In this research, we examine the effects of image restoration methods on image segmentation and develop a novel image partitioning model that integrates image restoration with the image segmentation process. Our proposed model combines image reconstruction to improve image clarity and edge definition, then applies graph segmentation based on a weighted graph that reflects image features. By conducting experiments and comparing the performance of the new model with the traditional graph segmentation method, we demonstrate that the model has the potential to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of image segmentation.

To enhance efficiency, Abstract Interpretation often employs over- or under-approximations that simplify input information, such as removing control flow details. Consequently, programs with minimal control flow changes, like loops, are represented as non-linear transformations, where the input simplifies to the output. A key strategy to improve over-approximation accuracy involves modeling these transformations as affine functions, which balance simplicity with control flow information retention better than non-linear functions. However, when solving for the parameters defining these affine functions, rising and falling phases are intertwined, making rising phase analysis challenging and computationally expensive due to synthesized control flow. This paper suggests separating rising and falling phases to streamline rising phase analysis. This separation can be achieved by modeling rising and falling phases as distinct affine functions of the program's execution duration, which reduces the required control flow information to start and end times. By utilizing existing solvers to ensure validity, this approach enhances the accuracy of over-approximations, which in turn tightens the constraints for static analysis. The proposed solution demonstrates significant potential through validated results on benchmark programs, which show up to 10 times faster rising phase analysis and 50 times total runtime improvements compared to current methods.

A key property of sound wave propagation through oxides, which can be topologically protected by this light, has the capability to facilitate the transmission of acoustic signals without disruption. The cross-polarized light field not only protects topological phase transitions but also protected phase boundaries promote the propagation of sound waves in directions opposite to each other. The experimentally verified phenomenon demonstrated that topological phonons can be controlled by light, providing theoretical backing for developing advanced acoustic devices utilizing this phenomenon.

Identifying outliers in a dataset is a critical challenge, especially when dealing with complex, non-Euclidean data. A novel approach using proxy graphs efficiently finds outliers in various data types by approximating empirical distance distributions on a proxy graph, such as a k-NN graph, instead of performing computationally expensive distance calculations. On typical datasets, this approach outperforms the brute-force method by over 100 times, while also delivering high accuracy, achieving approximately 95% accuracy in identifying outliers in multivariate data and anomaly points in images.

Our investigation involves the atom-field interaction when an atom is positioned in front of a slender metallic mirror. The vacuum electric field from the mirror induces motion, which in turn influences the atom's energy levels. Our calculation of the atom's emission spectrum is based on this induced movement. Since the mirror is extremely thin, it experiences a shift in its resonance frequencies. This enables us to consider the atom-mirror interaction by accounting for the mirror's mobility in addition to the atom's mobility. The case of a stationary atom is also revisited in this context. The long-time behavior of the electromagnetic emission of a two-level atom is examined in the case of its dipole moment being either aligned or perpendicular to the mirror surface. The role of the mode density of the vacuum and the electromagnetic coupling is clarified in this scenario. The calculated results are presented in the form of power spectra in both the far- and near-field zones. The comparison between these two cases and our previous study reveals distinct emission patterns. The mode density coupling is found to be affected by transverse Doppler broadening in the far-field zone.

When training graph models for decision-making tasks like credit scoring, ensuring these models don't discriminate against protected groups is crucial. While prior studies have tackled this by applying fairness constraints to node attributes, they overlook the natural hierarchy and organization within graphs. In reality, people are often connected based on their surrounding network, and it's this localized context that drives decision-making. Thus, we suggest comparing model predictions with those made by humans within each person's localized group, which we call localized fairness. We've developed a method to measure the fairness discrepancy between a model and human decision-making within these localized groups and derived an optimized algorithm for minimizing this discrepancy under mild assumptions. Our experiments demonstrate that this community-based fairness approach significantly outperforms traditional attribute-based fairness methods, delivering models that are both fair and predictive, as well as robust to manipulations aimed at manipulating the model's predictions to ensure fairness.

This work examines the kinetic reversible enzyme process $S + E \rightlefthas P + E$, with a focus on kinetic limits in terms of the variables representing substrate, enzyme, product, and their rates. To reach these kinetic limits quickly, researchers use an iterative approach, which involves an approximate solution to the kinetic process. This kinetic limit method relies on the inversion of certain matrices that product the relevant inverse matrices. Additionally, the study investigates the convergence of this iterative method.

Researchers investigated local 95% confidence intervals and exclusion limits for 8 simplified models of supersymmetry in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, with final states consisting of one or multiple jets and zero transverse momentum. The models, all decaying into a hidden sector, were examined in light of the latest data from the 13 TeV, 2015 collision year and a dedicated jet-tagging strategy. For simplified models involving a gluino, stop, and squark, spanning the full range of masses from 0 to 3000 GeV/c2 and no, single or divided supersymmetry, researchers found limits of approximately 720, 680, and 690 GeV, respectively. For models involving a simplified topcolor-SUSY scenario, researchers found limits of approximately 650, 640, and 660 GeV, respectively, and for models involving a simplified resonance scenario, researchers found limits of approximately 670, 660, and 680 GeV, respectively.

We introduce a new statistical measure, the Information Coefficient, which tracks how much better one random variable predicts another random variable compared to just using the average value of the second variable for prediction. By using the Information Coefficient, we propose a new concept, the Implicit Prediction Time Horizon, which represents the time it takes for the initial random variable to make the most accurate guess about the second one. We apply the Information Coefficient to the study of the Logical Expectation Theory on positive-skewed financial bubble models. Specifically, we examine two models: the Generalized Logistic-distributed bubble and the Generalized Gamma-distributed bubble. Our analysis shows that the Bessel Function is a key element in determining the Information Coefficient, which then informs the Implicit Prediction Time Horizon. Furthermore, we explore how changes in a model's parameters affect the Implicit Prediction Time Horizon.

The quantitative harmonic oscillator under specific conditions is a classic model in theoretical physics, often employed to illustrate various concepts, from its fundamental conceptions to complex measurements of coherence. Its simplicity allows researchers to test new techniques without the need for extensive numerical calculations. In this research, we present an introduction to path integral methods for driven quantum harmonic states, and use a current approach based on Wang-Landau to calculate the equilibrium partition function. Two Monte Carlo methods, Wang-Landau and Bruckner, were applied and compared for their efficiency. Two distinct sampling methods for spatial and momentum distributions were also investigated and found to yield consistent results, as were the results for the completeness check. Finally, we used the partition function to calculate quantum dynamics of coherence and found that decay in coherence occurs in both the short and long term.

E-commerce platforms often struggle with providing personalized recommendations,
despite the significant differences in consumer preferences.
The most effective recommendations are based on both product and
user similarities, and the integration of sentiment analysis can enhance
the accuracy of user preferences. Review-based recommendations can
effectively capture user preferences by analyzing the sentiment within
purchasing users' reviews and making them accessible to the model.
To this end, we propose a Sentiment - Interactive Fusion Network,
or SIFN, for review-based product recommendations and demonstrate
its success on two real-world datasets by considering the
user-product and user-user relationships and the influence of
sentiment on user preferences, all within a deep learning framework.
Through model swapping analysis and ablation studies, we validate the
efficacy of the proposed approach.

This work presents an innovative data augmentation technique for code-switched Arabic English text, which develops a language model that generates an unsupervised dictionary mapping Arabic words to their corresponding English equivalents. The method's effectiveness in code-switching relies on fine-tuning the language model with an approach similar to self-supervised learning. Initially, we examine the limitations of current LMs in code-switching patterns, which we then attempt to overcome by refining the pre-training objective of the model. Specifically, we modify the training process to capture these patterns. To validate the utility of the model, we examine its effects on two key tasks: context-based Arabic word translation and Arabic text classification. The results demonstrate that the model's predictions align closely with those from human translators and show that the data augmentation technique has proven valuable for real-world language translation and classification issues.

A topological group G has a certain type of topology, known as the Roelcke uniformity, when considering its continuous self-transformations. A distribution of tangent vectors at a particular point in another manifold is considered as a separate mathematical entity. If this manifold is compact, any distribution can be transformed into a compact group under the Schröder-Liebskind topology, which is different from the Roelcke topology. However, when the manifold has negative curvature, point evaluations remain non-compact under the Roelcke topology, which follows from their transformation capabilities. Moreover, when dealing with analytic diffeomorphisms, their orbit distributions are either finite or non-compact under the Roelcke topology.

We are examining string and superstring theories of connected branes, specifically the 19D and 10.9D superstring generalizations of the SU(2)xU(2)/U(1) coset, which are related to the U(1) instanton in the SU(2) group through generalized lambda deformations. These superstring theories exhibit a degree of simplicity akin to that of supergroup Wess-Zumino-Witten theories, yet the branes within these theories possess a degree of complexity that precludes this comparison. We are analyzing the properties of these branes, which can be either conformal or non-conformal, with a particular focus on two types of configurations: concentric and non-concentric.

To compare Tets/Hex to Hex meshes, a precise, low-bound metric is necessary, but existing research has established strict limits on the number of operations per simpler mesh element. This paper introduces a performance metric of "Tets/Hex to Hex," and while providing a positive outcome, it acknowledges the expense of this method. To improve weaker element shapes, a SplitHex algorithm is presented, utilizing sub-optimally positioned Coplanar Tetrahedra to divide the given Hexagon. Subsequently, the proposed method's efficacy is evaluated computationally, showcasing the benefits of using Tetrahedra to enhance Hex Meshes up to the given performance threshold.

Extracting relationships from text has numerous applications and is frequently encountered in everyday language. One common approach to doing so is using a encoder-decoder model, which is often paired with a classifier. However, our experiments indicate that this results in significant performance losses and inconsistent outcomes when dealing with varying amounts of data. Instead, we have found that a single neural network can be used for both relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction by designing a suitable loss function that combines objectives of both tasks. By integrating a knowledge graph, we enable the model to leverage additional context to fill in missing information, which allows it to generalize better to different levels of labeling. Additionally, we demonstrate in our findings that this approach yields substantial improvements over existing methods for both structured and unstructured datasets.

The converter delay (CD) is a crucial parameter in analyzing further advance optical communication systems employing coherent detection and digital signal processing. There are various digital optical formats, each requiring a unique CD value. This study provides a comprehensive analytical method for determining the converter delay, specifically tailored for standard 16-QAM systems with an unsymmetrical pulse shape, such as those featuring raised-cosine filtering with exponential tails. By facilitating an exact numerical solution, the proposed method enables, at a minimum, a precise approximation of the converter delay, allowing for the efficient computation of raised-cosine tail lengths. This method is implemented using Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolkit, allowing for the efficient computation of the converter delay.

We explore the connections between continuous reinforcement learning policies and their corresponding transitions between states. To capture a agent's robustness to small changes in the environment, such as low-resolution images in deep learning applications, we examine the relationships within state spaces that have varying levels of granularity. Our approach involves using probabilistic coarse-graining functions to map detailed states to less detailed ones, thereby allowing us to bound the differences between the original and coarse-grained transitions with probabilities. To demonstrate this concept, we focus on stochastic flow environments as examples of continuous reinforcement learning tasks and show how to derive upper-bounds on the discrepancies between detailed and coarse-grained transitions.

Research in primate brain anatomy has highlighted the significance of the superior temporal sulcus as a boundary separating animate from inanimate objects in the human temporal lobe. We investigated this animacy organizational pattern in human visual cortex by examining how the brain responds to different categories of stimuli. We collected fMRI data while subjects viewed various classes of stimuli and compared it to existing ventral temporal cortex connectivity data. Our findings suggest that the anatomical proximity of the superior temporal sulcus plays a pivotal role in the temporal lobe's representation of animacy.

In electromagnetic and elastodynamics, numerical predictions rely heavily on finite element methods, particularly for complex geometries, where the mesh arrangement plays a crucial role. However, traditional filtering methods like moving average, spline methods, and convex optimization filters often fail when dealing with irregular meshes, making arrangement-dependent simulations challenging. A new convex optimization filter has been developed to preserve mesh arrangement during filtering processes, effectively filtering out high-frequency errors or noise while ensuring the integrated values of the data remain unchanged. This novel filter has shown equivalence to the traditional moving average filter in regular grids, but with improved performance on geometry-dependent simulations, making it a valuable tool for a wide range of application scenarios.

Researchers have identified that some low-mass X-ray binaries experience quasi-periodic oscillations, appearing in two forms: type-A and type-C, which are related to different accretion flow phases. The transformation from type-C to type-A oscillations is associated with these systems evolving out of the hard X-ray state. In this study, we investigate the evolution of quasi-periodic oscillations in GX Per during its 2018 outburst and those related changes, using data from Insight-HXMT's XIS and MXRT instruments in the 2-10 keV and 3-25 keV energy bands respectively. The evolution of PQPO intensity and hardness, along other X-ray band parameters, are examined through detailed spectral analysis, along examining coronal development through variability and other processes. Our results show coronal growth, characterized by changes in X-ray band parameters, occurred before coronal development began, indicating matter accumulation, and then its movement towards the compact object. The spectral broadening of emission lines, which occurred, is attributed to the formation of a hot corona. The spectral broadening of emission lines, which occurred, is attributed to the formation of a hot corona.

A key challenge in developing socially autonomous robots is effectively learning tasks from humans that involve consistent and adaptive behavior. To address this, our research introduces an innovative method that utilizes transfer empowerment to consistently learn socially relevant tasks by leveraging observations of beneficial behaviors. By incorporating the demonstration of beneficial behaviors, we establish a foundation for developing adaptive behavior, ensuring that robots can reliably respond to partners' actions in various contexts. Through a combination of simulation and real-world experiments, we demonstrate that our proposed approach promotes socially dependable behavior, making it suitable for human-robot collaboration. Additionally, our experiments consistently show the effectiveness of transfer empowerment in transferring beneficial behaviors across multiple tasks, showcasing its value in shaping adaptable and reliable robotic behavior.

Determining the identity of unknown substances, even with minimal or no initial knowledge, is a common challenge in spectroscopy. A breakthrough solution has been developed using contrastive learning and physics-based simulations to identify substances based on spectral signatures from molecular and atomic compositions. This method effectively compares simulated signatures of known substances with experimental data to determine their identity by matching their features. It outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in frequency and Raman spectrometry by accurately identifying substances with few or no prior observations.

This text begins by introducing the concept of Lie 2-algebras, which can be derived from Lie 2-algebras, 2-Lie algebras, or strict Lie 2-algebras, which are all equivalent through various constructions involving L∞-algebras and Vinberg constructions. The text then explores Vinberg's construction specifically for Lie 2-algebras derived from Lie bialgebras and their cobrazits, as well as focusing on 2-Lie algebras and their relation to Courant algebroids and 2-plectic manifets. Finally, the text provides examples of Lie 2-algebras constructed from Poisson groups and their connections to Lie 2-algebras derived from Lie bialgebras.

Discrepancy in keypoint detection and keypoint matching results often stems from the fact that keypoint detection is typically carried out with different camera relative prior information compared to keypoint matching. This paper proposes an alternative, detector-free approach, called LoFTR, for resolving local features in images. This novel model leverages self- and cross-attention mechanisms of the transformer architecture to incorporate camera relative prior information. Moreover, LoFTR achieves superior performance in both dense keypoint correspondence and scene correspondence due to the adaptability of the cross-attention mechanism, which allows for the incorporation of different types of geometric prior knowledge. Experimental findings demonstrate that LoFTR outperforms other models in various aspects and geometric conditions and also exhibits enhanced scene correspondence capabilities in multi-view settings and broader camera calibrations.

This paper aims to recognize and mitigate bias in the measurement of solar vector magnetic fields. By comparing the magnetic field, or B-field, data from the vector magnetograms of the Sun's disk provided by the Helioseismic and Differential Imager (HSDI) and the Vector Solar Magnetic Field Measurement (VSM) instruments, we discovered a notable disparity. The HSDI's B-field is found to be 15-20% more than that of the VSM across the entire 0-8000 Gauss (G) range, with the disparity being more pronounced at higher field strengths. Although the vector magnetic field data provided by HSDI and VSM have consistent direction, their magnitudes differ significantly. By applying a piecewise linear approximation, we have successfully reduced the HSDI's B-field data to align with that of the VSM, resulting in a notable decrease in the root mean square error (RMSE) between the two datasets.
