To minimize real-time electricity costs, an innovative demand side control approach employs a game theory framework in which consumers engage in strategic planning of their future energy needs. The proposed system allows consumers to autonomously decide on their optimal charging times by simulating different scenarios, effectively reducing real-time energy expenses through strategic scheduling. By implementing this approach within the Markov Decision Process framework, consumers can iteratively develop strategies that not only lower their energy costs but also promote energy efficiency in real-time. Through game theory analysis, we demonstrate the convergence of this system towards an optimal outcome known as a Pure Nash Equilibrium. Our numerical study showcases the efficacy of this approach in substantially reducing consumers' real-time energy costs, with significant cost savings observed as a direct result of strategic demand side control.

A recent analysis of the Gravitational Potential Theory (GPT) has led to the discovery of new solutions for the gravitational field, specifically for the interior of stars and compact objects like black holes and dwarf galaxies, due to their unique 1-form potential. However, the electromagnetic influences on the gravitational field in Rastall Theory (RT) have not been explored, and the effect on the construction of Hawking radiation in certain compact objects has not been studied. Therefore, this study aims to delve into the construction of Hawking radiation around a family of charged objects, specifically the extended Schwarzschild-de Sitter (SDS) and extended Reissner-Nordstrom-de Sitter (RNSD) black holes, within the context of both GPT and RT. By comparing these objects and their properties, we can determine how the presence of an additional 1-form potential in GPT affects Hawking radiation and whether it is physically justified. Our results show that GPT can lead to a decrease in Hawking temperature, and thus, more efficient Hawking radiation emission, compared to the standard RT, and that both GPT and RNSD black holes emit more radiation and last longer than extended SDS black holes.

We develop methods to estimate spectral distributions in the context of the Hilbert space $H$, where we establish a fundamental link between spectral distributions, projections, and self-adjoint operators on $H$. Furthermore, we introduce two key theorems, establishing upper and lower bounds for spectral distributions in the Ergodic Theorem by von Neumann, which reveal the convergence speeds of mean-square for weakly periodic sequences in $H$, while offering practical criteria for identifying periodic or almost periodic sequences.

The recently acquired spectra from Gaia's BP/RP photometers prove to be highly effective in determining the chemical composition of metal-poor stars. A specific technique has been created, which facilitates the determination of the logarithmic abundance of a crucial element, iron. This technique can accurately estimate metal abundance for a broad range of temperatures. It relies on restricted, temperature-appropriate sets of spectra, which are matched to synthetic spectra, from which iron abundances are obtained. It doesn't depend on precise distance or radial velocity measurements. It has been tested on 230000 stars and compared with existing datasets. It doesn't rely on prior abundance data or its associated uncertainties. It can accurately predict iron abundances from other datasets. It doesn't show any systematic errors. It's particularly effective (no more than 0.05 dex) for stars with effective temperatures between 4000 and 6200 K. It's also useful for estimating abundance of a second element (e.g. alpha element) when combined with certain spectral features. It's straightforward to implement and can be used to determine abundance of any element for a broad range of temperatures. It's made accessible through an online platform. It's poised to provide valuable insights into the chemical evolution of the Milky Way. It's well-positioned to contribute significantly to galactic archaeology.

Every year, more than 400 million hectares and 3.6 million tons of CO2 are consumed by intense wildfires globally. These fires disproportionately affect developing nations, but data availability remains limited, hindering accurate monitoring. An analysis of fire data from the MODIS satellite and land cover information reveals that fire seasons are predictable, occurring during dry periods when vegetation is most susceptible to ignition. This study defines and quantifies the intensity of fire seasons and their key characteristics, enabling them to be forecast a year in advance with 70% accuracy.

Researchers have developed various metrics to evaluate language complexity but there's a lack of consensus on their definitions. This study examines and compares different metrics for known languages and the Glottolm language simulator to understand their underlying concepts. By comparing the correlation of 12 metrics, we observe that certain combinations of them measure similar aspects of a language. Furthermore, the study validates 6 of these metrics using a diverse dataset and evaluates their reliability through reliability tests. Notably, the study reveals that the underlying concept of each metric may not necessarily align with its original purpose, underscoring the need for rigorous metric validation in linguistic research.

Galaxy cluster lensing effects hold potential to uncover signs of self-interacting dark matter beyond the capabilities of the Abell cluster lensing challenge.  However, the actual self-interaction cross-section between dark matter particles remains uncertain and difficult to determine directly from observations in galaxy clusters.  In the process of investigating how this interaction affects the angular correlation of caustics in multiple-lens systems within clusters, it becomes apparent that this method can indirectly increase the sensitivity to self-interacting dark matter.  The phenomenon of small-scale gravitational magnification in clusters may provide an effective means to detect self-interacting dark matter with typical interaction strengths around 1 picobarn.  The procedure involves comparing the observed positions of caustics to those predicted in a standard cold dark matter model and then evaluating how these positions shift due to the influence of dark matter scattering processes.  The procedure can also be applied to galaxy groups, where it may provide further insight into self-interacting dark matter's properties and detect typical interaction strengths around 10 picobarn.  The phenomenon of small-scale gravitational magnification in galaxy clusters can be observed through multi-colour imaging of arc-like features and caustic structures.  Observations reveal that caustics tend to appear bluer than the flux magnified by the cluster lens, and that the flux magnification effect increases with wavelength.  This effect is attributed to the influence of gaseous scattering in the cluster lens, which can cause caustics to appear

High-dimensional data analysis can be difficult due to its inherent complexity and scarcity of samples. A common approach to address this is to reduce its dimensionality. In this study, we investigate the effects of using lower-dimensional data subsets on clustering performance, specifically under the stochastic block model. Our theoretical results reveal that even small increases in data dimensionality can significantly impact clustering accuracy, suggesting that highly dimensional data leads to better outcomes. This finding is further validated by simulation results. Consequently, our study provides direct clustering theory for stochastic block models with high-dimensional data, which can notably expand its applicability.

A new class of functions for identifying non-Gaussian sources in independent component analysis has been created. These functions combine nonlinearity with specific properties to handle Gaussian noise, particularly in the context of mixed-arithmetic precisions. The functions' effectiveness was demonstrated through a simulated rapid ICA approach, achieving better results than existing methods while precisions switch between 32-bit and 7-bit formats.

Real-time traffic incident monitoring is a critical requirement for effective incident management, and geotagged social platforms like Foursquare provide up-to-date information about traffic conditions that can be leveraged for monitoring. By incorporating social data with traffic incident description, we can define an incident identification model called I^2SG, and conduct a large-scale study across California's major highways. This empirical analysis allows us to compare the temporal and spatial accuracy of social data with traditional incident detection methods, and proposes an operational framework for incident management.

This research focuses on the following fractional-type elliptic problem: $$\left\{\begin{array}{ll} -\Delta u + \frac{c_1}{\mathrm{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)}u = f & \mathrm{in}\,\,\Omega, \\
u = 0 & \mathrm{on}\,\,\partial\Omega, \end{array}\right.$$ where $\Omega$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n\geq 2$. We'll investigate this problem by applying variational methods and proving the existence of two distinct solutions, given certain conditions on parameter $c_1$ and function $f$. Our analysis also includes examining the behavior of these solutions when the force term $f$ approaches a surface measure supported on $\partial\Omega$, along with deriving the corresponding convergence results.

First, we employed evolutionary predictions to choose an initial set of 500 Y-Co-B compounds for structural exploration, for which we computed the total energies using the DFT-LDA method as a quick approximation. This resulted in a selection of 100 low-energy structures. Next, we performed a comprehensive analysis using DFT-GGA to filter out instabilities and made predictions based on machine learning, ultimately yielding 18 compounds of interest. These 18 Y-Co-B compounds were then validated experimentally, confirming the accuracy of the initial screening process. The 18 Y-compounds exhibit cobalt-rich compositions and predominantly adopt hexagonal structures, showcasing various magnetic characteristics. The compounds of significance comprise stable alloys and the 14 distinct stoichiometric configurations explored in this study.

In the field of display advertising, the demand for risk-aware bidding strategies is on the rise, where a key objective is to maximize overall revenue while adhering to an investor's budget and other constraints. Existing research has typically focused on offline settings, where the click-through and conversion rates are pre-known and unchanging. In real-world online scenarios, however, product pages exhibit varying levels of attractiveness to users and their actual outcomes remain uncertain. To address this issue, we've developed an innovative online bidding framework that takes into consideration not only the budget constraint but also the variability in product Attractiveness, the probability of a click resulting in a conversion, and the conversion itself. Our novel approach builds upon the Gittins index policy and introduces the AGGI policy, allowing bidding agents to adapt to online scenarios efficiently. Through both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations, the AGGI policy has demonstrated superior performance compared to existing online policies and the previously proposed offline-based algorithms.

Regions of negative Wigner function are often attributed to quantum complexity, limiting classical phase space descriptions. Our work demonstrates a connection between quantum processes that lack classical analogues and the occurrence of negative Wigner function values. By showing how the back-action avoidance criterion determines when quantum measurements have no effect on a system's state, we establish its relationship with Wigner function positivity. Our results specifically demonstrate a link between lossy measurements resulting in negativity and destructive Wigner phase-averaging effects that cancel out back-action. Consequently, our findings reveal the interplay between Wigner negativity and essential quantum characteristics such as intractability and the absence of classical counterparts.

Our research introduces a novel approach to boosting quantum key distribution (QKD) efficiency, especially when using repeater-based techniques and non-uniform random phase encoding. We successfully implemented a quantum enhanced key distribution protocol in a simulation with a fully non-uniform random source and non-binary detection, achieving a 30 km secure connection. The efficiency was significantly improved compared to traditional binary encoding with uniform sources, which had a secure connection limited to 10 km. Our findings show that quantum enhanced key distribution is highly adaptable, especially in environments with varying noise levels, making it suitable for diverse applications.

This research paper investigates the properties of a particular type of curve, a timelike Bertrand curve, within a non-Euclidean geometric framework. A mathematical condition is derived and subsequently used to identify specific subspaces that contain these curves, namely the timelike screen isotropic subspaces and the timelike lightlike isotropic subspaces in three-dimensional spacetime.

Recent research by Fontes and Toledo (2019) introduced novel characterization results focused on linear combinations of independent Feller diffusions with varying initial conditions. This paper builds upon their work by further examining Feller diffusion combinations, specifically analyzing sample distributions and providing practical applications. We derive nonnegative combination scalars and explore their implications, such as the sum of standard Fox-Arlington random variables and a representation of the generalized lambda distribution.

We introduce an efficient diagrammatic approach for analyzing multi-photon scattering of waveguide quantum electrodynamics systems, which expands upon existing diagrammatic techniques used in quantum optics. Our method facilitates straightforward calculation of a system's multi-photon scattering matrix by mapping it to a two-dimensional photon world line lattice. We illustrate this approach's effectiveness through application to a symmetric double qubit setup, where we compute its full six-photon scattering matrix. Furthermore, we investigate the striking single-qubit-dependent chiral behavior exhibited by this system, discovering an unexpected phenomenon where multi-qubit states undergo significant, diagrammatically-predictable transformations.

In the context of dark energy with coupled fermions, we explore the late-time dynamics in a four-dimensional space-time with transient cosmological constants. Our work demonstrates that, depending on the fermion density, the cosmological parameters can either stabilize or oscillate over time, thereby having a significant impact on the dark energy distribution and structural development. Moreover, by separating the dark energy distribution into even and odd components, we demonstrate that the coupled dark energy behaves like spin-dependent diffusion. Our findings reveal that coupled dark matter and dark energy play a significant role in the cosmological structural evolution.

This note is based on the children's mathematics competition (Festive Mathematics) organized by Moscow Schools for talent identification. The competition included the following problem: Prove that for any positive integer $n$, the sum $1^k + 2^k + \ldots + (2n-1)^k + (2n)^k$ is divisible by $n$, and find the largest $k$ such that the sum $1^k + 2^k + \ldots + n^k$ is divisible by $n(n-1)/2$ for all $n \geq 2$. The solution to this problem can be achieved through a property of Faulhaber polynomials and the application of Bernoulli numbers and their properties developed by Euler.

For terahertz communication systems requiring massive parallelism, a crucial challenge is achieving efficient low-cost detection without relying on highly complex coherent processes. Traditional differential detection, while avoiding phase tracking, suffers from being a nonlinear distortion that necessitates equalization. We propose an enhancement to standard non-coherent differential detection of continuous phase modulation by transforming the system's characteristics into linear properties through differentialization. In contrast to the conventional approach where each symbol is independently encoded and decoded, our method encodes multiple symbols collectively and processes them jointly. Notably, our enhanced detector, defined as DkDD, can decode k consecutive symbols and achieve equivalent performance to coherent detection in indistinct channels. In well-conditioned channels, our detector outperforms the conventional DD method with up to 0.3dB improved SNR efficiency and, crucially, its complexity is lower than that of a Viterbi equalizer. Furthermore, our detector shows resilience to phase noise and experiences no performance decline when the number of symbols is 2.

A crucial step in obtaining reward functions that accurately represent user preferences is conducting comparisons between videos to guide reward learning. However, existing methods require significant user effort to evaluate and are often limited to online settings. To address this, we have developed a method that efficiently organizes and presents video options in clusters, enabling users to compare multiple scenarios simultaneously and reduce evaluation time. The proposed approach, based on visual clustering, can be applied to both online and offline settings, but is particularly well-suited for offline environments where it allows users to complete all comparisons within a single session. Through extensive user studies, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our system in reducing evaluation time while maintaining or even surpassing the overall comparison quality in offline settings. The proposed system is available at https://github.com/microsoft/VECRA.

This study examines the impact of noncommutative time-space on the spin and orbital structure of the nucleon, specifically exploring how the noncommutative parameter influences the nucleon's mass generation through a generalized model of the nucleon. In the noncommutative framework, we investigated how the nucleon's mass is generated by quark and diquark components using the constituent quark model. Our findings indicate that the noncommutative parameter has a significant effect on the nucleon mass, particularly in the case of the nucleon mass where the contribution from quarks and anti-quarks differs significantly. However, in the case of the diquark mass, the contribution from quarks and anti-quarks are nearly identical. This work sheds light on the potential role of noncommutative time-space on the spin and orbital structure of the nucleon.

The topological edge phenomenon occurs when a modified code, defined on the boundary of higher-dimensional systems, cannot be derived from the bulk properties of the bulk code's tight-binding model. This phenomenon was discovered in cases where the bulk and edge code's spatial dimensions mismatch by one. A more complex instance arises when bulk and edge code dimensionalities don't align, which our study investigates in the context of code models where the dimensionalities do mismatch. A revised version of the toric code on a 3D cubic lattice, built using a partial spin ice model on the boundary, is examined. This study finds that this construction does not comply with typical code model methods for topologically ordered systems. Consequently, we look for an explanation of the phenomenon in terms of symmetry-protected topological properties of the bulk.

We introduce a new class of complex perturbations of real, disorder-matrix types with limited range and calculate the adjusted eigenvalue density as given by the Pfister-Haake-Siedler formula from 1993. This computation significantly advances our understanding of the spectrum of large, randomly perturbed band matrices, particularly when their size approaches infinity and perturbations occur at various distances. Focusing on the one-dimensional case of infinite range perturbations, our findings show that the universal edge eigenvalue density derived in2020 is accurately represented using the sigma-model approximation, similarly validated in subsequent studies. The achieved level of precision for finite-rank perturbations surpasses previous results and significantly improves upon existing methods, thereby stimulating further discussions within the statistical random matrix theory community.

The success of conversation-based models largely relies on the quality of pre-trained language representations.  However, conventional pre-training models are limited to language aspects and fail to capture conversational context. Additionally, they pre-trained without considering the unique demands of conversation understanding tasks. To address these issues, we propose a novel pre-training method that considers semantic, pragmatic, and conversation-related meanings. For this purpose, we design a new model called MEPRa, which uses in-context information and conversation history to bridge the gap between language and conversation. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through improved performance across three downstream conversation understanding tasks, utilizing history-independent and conversation-specific pre-trained models, thereby validating the importance of meaningful-based pre-training and our proposed model architecture.

Many computer algorithms operate as opaque, unexplainable black boxes, which poses a significant challenge in understanding the connections between inputs and outputs, particularly for humans. This issue is of great interest to researchers in cognitive science. This study presents a comprehensive framework, CIB, aimed at quantifying the complexity of human-interpretable algorithms. The primary goal of CIB is to develop a reliable metric for measuring cognitive intricacy and elucidating the interconnections between human and machine learning interpretations. This framework consists of two parts: theoretical modeling of human learning and a search for optimal metrics to evaluate human-interpretable algorithms. This paper comprehensively discusses various potential metrics, evaluates their performance, and presents initial applications for this purpose. Furthermore, this paper explores the relationship between human and machine learning within the context of algorithmic interpretability.

The Isolation Forest is a well-established algorithm for detecting anomalies, but its underlying theory is complex and implementation challenges arise. To address this, the TiWS-iForest, the first lightweight, high-accuracy C implementation of the Isolation Forest, has been developed. It features extensive code comments, a straightforward design, and a minimal dependency on external libraries. The TiWS-iForest outperforms existing C implementations in anomaly detection accuracy, surpassing them significantly in benchmark tests while demonstrating exceptional adaptability in resource-constrained environments, including embedded devices and tiny machine learning settings. Its integration with WebAssembly and the ARM Cortex-M architecture further enhances its portability and efficiency.

A novel time-reparameterization for the Poisson process, specifically for any non-decreasing, absolutely continuous function spanning the entire positive real axis, has been established, leading to the derivation of the corresponding compensated random measure. This measure is used in extreme value theory, particularly in modeling minimum values, and the technique is applied in a Bayesian context with the case of normal Poisson process parameterization examined.

The fundamental optical theorem connects the average cross-section to a scattering amplitude at zero angle, leading to constraints on this average cross-section due to analyticity and unitarity. Historically, research revealed that specific regions in parameters $s$ and $t$ exhibit stationary average cross-sections. This study aims to adapt existing averages to demonstrate additional stationary points at $t\neq0$. The investigation also assesses a new average that covers the entire range of $t$ values. The findings indicate that a combination of different averages can be utilized to extract the $t$-component of the forward scattering amplitude at $t\neq0$ without increased error margins.

This study presents COMET-ATOMIC, an innovative benchmark and task evaluation framework for evaluating deep learning models of common sense knowledge networks. Unlike previous works, COMET-ATOMIC offers a substantial dataset, a unique statistical analysis tool, and a comprehensive set of tasks, enabling performance comparison between ATOMIC's original BERT-based network and COMET-ATOMIC's network built using BERT and XLM-R, the latter being a multilingual transformer, to highlight the potential for improving common sense knowledge network inference. Our analysis reveals that incorporating word embeddings and using XLM-R results in significant improvements over previous work, and between ATOMIC and COMET-ATMIC, the two models, the latter outperforms in multiple aspects.

This paper presents and discusses the analysis pipeline used for processing data from the Hi-GAL survey, which targeted star-forming regions in the Galaxy. Utilizing the Herschel Space Observatory, data were collected at frequencies of 350 and 500 micrometers. A significant challenge posed by the Hi-GAL survey's large data volume was overcoming storage constraints. To address this issue, researchers created a reduction pipeline at the Level 0 stage, efficiently minimizing data size and swiftly relocating data to analysis facilities. The paper details the reduction pipeline's design, development, and application, showcasing成果 from data processing and scientific analysis.

The globular cluster NGC 2808 exhibits a notable metallicity spread within its horizontal branch, a phenomenon that can be attributed to multiple generations of stars. We have determined the elemental ratios of key elements for horizontal branch members in NGC 2808, including iron and alpha, magnesium, calcium, neon, oxygen, carbon, and helium using the TESSEL code. Our research utilized high-resolution spectra from the HIRES and VIMOS-UVES instruments. A notable finding is the observed metallicity differences between the red and blue horizontal branch members, a distinction that aligns with previous studies in NGC 2808. We have discovered a correlation between horizontal branch morphologies and the [O/Fe] and [Mg/Fe] ratios for both the blue and red branches. We have also found a correlation between the [Ca/Fe] and [neon/iron] ratios for the red and blue branches, while discovering a spread in the [neon/iron] and [calcium/iron] elemental ratios. Our research contributes to our understanding of the metallicity spread within NGC 2808, a cluster that is thought to have been formed from multiple generations of stars with varying metallicity levels.

A numerical study of entropic forces in a single file diffusion (SFD) scenario has been undertaken by analyzing the initial exit time duration and speed distributions. The entropic forces in this model arise from configurations where a particle can exit the system. The study demonstrates that these entropic effects significantly influence the initial exit time duration, speed, and their corresponding distributions, influencing the transition from the SFD regime to the free diffusion regime. The study employs the concept of a coarse-grained configuration entropy and compares the theoretical and simulation results, finding agreement between the two, particularly at low filling fractions, but a discrepancy at high filling fractions.

Quantum mechanics poses challenges to the concept of Bayes' Theorem, particularly in handling indeterminate knowledge and inconsistent information density matrices. This work showcases how the quantum version of Bayes' Theorem addresses these limitations, ensuring consistency in information updates for scenarios involving mixed and pure states, as well as non-distinct initial conditions. In these scenarios, the quantum formula accurately recovers the Schrödinger and Bayes' equations, validating its reliability and providing a broader understanding of information updates in quantum physics.

Building upon prior research by the authors, we derive an expression for the energy density of quark-gluon plasma in the presence of a finite magnetic field. This new formula accounts for the effects of a finite chemical potential. When combined with the stochastic dynamics of magnetic flux tubes, our findings suggest that a finite magnetic field will have a more significant impact on the expansion rate of the quark-meson system in the early stages of system expansion. This effect is notably more pronounced in the first few fm/c of system evolution, a critical stage corresponding to two-flavor hadronic flow in nuclear collisions at mid-energy energies.

It is established that the non-trivial cohomology groups of the Steenrod algebra over $\mathbb{F}_2$ consist of polynomial generators. Building on P. Ni's method in \cite{P}, an algorithm is proposed to identify these generators in any specific case. As a result, the exact linear representatives of the Steenrod algebra's $\mathbb{F}_2$ cohomology groups are determined.

A novel Lyman-α filter, filter-1, has been developed to modify the transmission characteristics of the Hubble Space Telescope and enable Lyman-UV photometry across a broader range of redshifts up to 40. This novel filter enhances the detection capabilities of both the Wide Field Camera 3 and Wide Field Camera 3/Spectrograph Unit 3. When compared to existing color standards, this novel filter exhibits similarities to the Schlegel (1992) $u^*$ and $V$ photometric systems, as well as the SDSS $u'$ and the Spitzer/WISE color $W1-W2$. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the incorporation of this novel filter significantly increases the detection capabilities of HST by expanding the observable redshift range, increasing the detection probability of Ks > 26.5 by 100%, and expanding the detection capabilities of WFC3/SDSS-S3 by up to 50% for Ks > 26.5.

This research investigates the issue of regulated output synchronization in interconnected multi-node networks that share a degree of symmetry. By leveraging the eigenvalue decomposition of symmetric adjacency matrices, the paper proposes ideal control strategies using a class of invertible graph filters. Notably, the control gains are independent of inter-node coupling. To address this problem, the paper also introduces an optimization-based design method for custom-adapted graph filters that approach the performance of the implemented strategies, along with explicit performance evaluation metrics for the output synchronization error dynamics under tailored graph filters. This study also demonstrates the effective application of the designed graph filters to large-scale network settings with symmetric connectivity.

Retrieving and analyzing information from large collections of images has become increasingly crucial, driven by applications in computer vision and social media analysis. A crucial challenge in image retrieval is effectively searching through and analyzing unstructured visual content. Traditional indexing methods, designed for structured text, do not extend naturally to unstructured images, making this task even more complex. To address this issue, researchers have explored the concept of extending the indexing process to create dynamic, visual representations, called "indexing pictures," which describe the characteristics of larger images, such as photographs or video frames. These visual representations, called "indexing pictures," enable researchers to convert large sequences of images into a single image, which can then be analyzed and interpreted, similar to traditional image analysis methods. In this paper, we discuss the theory and methodology behind creating dynamic indexing pictures, showcasing its applications across various domains and highlighting its limitations.

This paper introduces Variflow, a research-driven software evaluation tool that assesses the Fejzo paper's coreless encryption techniques in real-world settings. Our research, rooted in the Fejzo findings, reveals that channel estimation errors significantly impact cryptographic strength in real-world scenarios. Although Fejzo's simulations indicate high channel capacity, it's limited by its reliance on low verification error rates, making it impractical for real-world applications where verification error rates are generally higher. Variflow, on the other hand, accurately reflects these rates, revealing them to be a critical factor in channel capacity and overall cryptographic strength. Consequently, Fejzo's proposed channel coding methods, which are derived from high-error-rate scenarios, may not be applicable to actual communications settings. Moreover, the presence of channel keying in these setups results in multiple verification error rates for each transmitted message, with only the most favorable rate being utilized in capacity calculations. This approach is at odds with standard communication protocols, which typically employ the most unreliable verification outcome to ensure a higher likelihood of correct message reception in case of channel disturbances. Consequently, the encryption techniques introduced by Fejzo appear to be unsuitable for secure real-world communications.

We offer a comprehensive theory of the uniform movement in a potential field that varies and also consider scenarios where it does not have a consistent direction. quasisoliton solutions in these systems are analyzed. It is demonstrated that a unique condition can be met in washboard energy curves, allowing for the creation of solitons with a specific and finite energy level. When in a stable state, the soliton's center remains aligned with the potential's axis, and its profile remains consistent. It is shown that the one-dimensional non-relativistic sine-Gordon model and relativistic versions are isomorphic to non-relativistic systems with different washboard energies. We establish a general equation to calculate the surface velocity of solitons in these systems. Additionally, the study explores two situations where the potential has no consistent direction. In the first scenario, the soliton's profile does not remain consistent and its energy increases. In the second scenario, the soliton exhibits periodic motion. The findings in these systems are compared with one-dimensional relativistic models.

To estimate impulse response functions, we present a new approach called AdaLPRO, which enhances the existing local projections estimator by making the coefficients in a polynomial flexible. Adapted polyreg estimates IRFs and their accompanying uncertainty levels more accurately. Simulations and real-world data analyses demonstrate that AdaLPRO outperforms the traditional LPRO estimator and other established baseline estimators. Our findings show that traditional econometric shrieke calculations tend to overestimate information uncertainty.

We present a novel approach to studying the interaction between a charged particle and electromagnetic vacuum fluctuations. Our method involves a dynamic transformation that causes the particle to move in a gyrotropic pattern in response to the vacuum's influence. The resulting classical angular momentum possessed by the charge is counterbalanced by a counterpart in the vacuum, ensuring the overall system maintains its zero angular momentum state. Consequently, the vacuum acquires a non-zero angular momentum value, which can be viewed as the cost of disrupting the equilibrium state of the vacuum. Our work conveys a tangible sense of the angular momentum inherent in the vacuum and offers a fresh perspective on a fundamental property of the vacuum through the lens of a basic physical process.

The traditional approach to Named Entity Classification, which relies on coarse-grained detection, often misses out on detailed information that can be crucial for various applications. In response, a refinement-based approach is proposed, which first uses a base model to identify potential entity spans and then employs a hyperbolic graph network to narrow down and enhance these predictions. In addition to refinement, this method leverages hyperbolic geometry's ability to model hierarchical relationships, which is particularly beneficial for handling the inherent hierarchy of detailed entity types. Our approach, FGNET-RH, incorporates pre-trained language models and hyperbolic graph networks to conduct fine-grained NER. Experimental results on the WSD and WIKI NER datasets showcase the effectiveness of FGNET-RH, outperforming existing methods and highlighting its potential for applications that require precise entity information.

The second Hankel determinant for functions with the general class $\mathcal{S}$ and functions belonging to the unit ball $U$ in the theory of univalent functions has garnered significant interest among researchers, particularly concerning its upper limit. A notable distinction exists in that, while the extreme value problem for the class $\mathcal{S}$ is still unresolved, it has been fully resolved for the subclass $U$ in recent years. In recent studies by Precious et al., the second Hankel determinant for the class $\mathcal{S}$ was discussed, relying on assumptions such as boundedness of $\alpha_4$ and applying subordination to $\frac{1+z}{1-z}$. In particular, Precious employed these assumptions to derive an estimate for $H_2$, but it was subsequently discovered that applying subordination to $\frac{1+z}{1-z}$ was unnecessary for establishing that estimate, and that it could lead to suboptimal bounds for $H_2$ in the absence of $\alpha_4$ being bounded. In the current study, the author revisits the estimation problem for $H_2$ for the general class $\mathcal{S}$ and the subclass $U$, ultimately deriving distinct, yet tighter, estimates for the various instances of $H_2$.

Emerging technologies like virtualization and cloud computing have enabled the efficient utilization of underused resources in traditional data centers. However, managing resources in these environments remains challenging. In response, the Industry 4.0 framework proposes an innovative approach, employing the Internet of Things (IoT) to bridge the gap between physical and digital worlds, enabling improved resource management. This paper showcases the potential of Prepartition, an innovative load distribution strategy that can be used in VM provisioning for data center management within the Industry 4.0 framework. By preemptively reallocating resources based on predicted workload patterns, Prepartition minimizes service disruptions and improves overall efficiency.

In many strategic interactions where multiple equilibrium solutions can arise, agents often struggle to choose the most suitable equilibrium in order to achieve the best possible outcome. Most current research utilizes handcrafted features, heuristics, or signal-broadcasting methods to resolve this ambiguity. However, recent studies have shown that deep learning models, when incorporating attention mechanisms, can successfully resolve such ambiguity without relying on heuristics or signal exchange. Inspired by the success of attention mechanisms, we introduce a novel concept where agents learn to foresee equilibrium states by utilizing a novel architecture known as a Fixed Point Network (FPN). FPN architecture combines a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) layer with a U-net generator and an adversarial discriminator, allowing it to learn an empirical fixed point function that serves as a useful heuristic for selecting equilibrium equilibrium. Notably, FPN architecture exhibits its versatility by being successfully applied to both single-shot learning tasks involving non-cooperative games and multi-shot learning tasks involving complex strategic games such as those incorporating public goods, signaling models, and entry deterrence models. FPN architecture also performs well across various machine learning paradigms and achieves remarkable results, achieving a 0.011 mean squared error (MSE) on the most challenging entry-deterrence model, a significant improvement over the baseline model's 0.07 MSE.

This research investigates the notion of causal influence, particularly in terms of its potential to predict future events or its relationship with entropy. A novel metric for predicting future events has been developed and proven to be constrained by the mutual information between causal factors and the predicted outcome. Additionally, the metric's robustness to noise was assessed through simulations. A new, randomized method for identifying significant causal factors was also proposed. These methods were then put into practice to rank the most influential genes associated with two bladder cancer subtypes, using publicly available, transcript-level data.

This study explores the implementation of predictive control in safeguarding critical infrastructures from intense cyber-physical attacks. When faced with unexpected attack conditions, the original model of the system becomes inaccurate. To adapt to this new reality, an adaptive predictive control framework is initially utilized. However, due to the intricate computations involved, this approach may not be economically viable. To address this issue, the paper develops a simplified representation of the system dynamics under attack, allowing for predictive control to effectively conceal and contain the attack. The accuracy of this simplified model, in turn, facilitates the estimation of actual system states. Consequently, a hybrid strategy is developed, combining adaptive control and signal measurement to optimize the performance of the system during cyber-physical attacks.

This research presents GAE-ISumm, a highly effective English abstractive summarization model, which we have modified to accommodate the unique characteristics of Indian languages. Utilizing a unique, large-scale dataset constructed from contemporary news articles, experimental results demonstrate that GAE-ISumm outperforms other non-monitored and heavily guided models on 26 Indian language datasets, achieving a highest score of 36.66 for泰米尔语 (Tamil). Additionally, Tiberius, another implementation of the model, attains an impressive score of 35.96 for Kannada. The accompanying code and resources can be accessed via the provided GitHub link.

Assume $R$ is an exchange ring satisfying the left and right Pseudo-Fuchsian conditions. We define a S-ring $\mathcal{S}$ of group $G$ as noetherian if the set of $G$-invariant submodules of $\mathbb{V}$ is noetherian. An $S$-ring $\mathcal{S}$ is classified as noetherian if every $G$-invariant submodule in $\mathbb{V}$ is a direct sum of irreducible $S$-modules. We establish that $\mathcal{S}$ having noetherian type on a vector space $\mathbb{V}$ implies that $\mathcal{S}$ is noetherian. Moreover, we demonstrate that if $\mathcal{S}$ is noetherian, the lattice of $G$-invariant submodules in $\mathbb{V}$ being noetherian necessitates that $\mathcal{S}$'s factor system $\mathcal{S}_0$ is also noetherian.

We used Very Large Telescope data to study the orbital characteristics of hidden objects associated with five stars that appear to exhibit accelerated motion. By analyzing the spectrum of hidden objects, we determined the minimum masses of the objects in four of the five systems, providing a crucial constraint on the objects' properties. Our analysis revealed the minimum masses of hidden objects in systems V612 Mon, HD 158258, and V470 Car, as well as setting a mass limit for hidden companions of V682 Ori, and confirmed the hidden object in this system cannot be a stellar black hole.

A widely accepted approach for unsupervised learning in deep learning is the use of autoencoders. The Variational Autoencoder (VAE) model, an unsupervised autoencoder variant, has been extensively used for data representation and missing value imputation. The VAE model minimizes the square difference of the input and output data by applying stochastic sampling to the network. However, due to its objective function's specific form, optimizing the VAE model can be challenging. This work introduces a novel VAE model that bypasses the drawbacks of the traditional VAE model. Our proposed model, called the Minimal Square VAE, removes the stochastic layer and replaces the KL divergence loss with a new regularizer. This model retains the core principles of VAEs while streamlining its structure. Our experiments demonstrate that the new model outperforms the traditional VAE in multiple areas, including its ability to prevent overfitting, prevent mode collapse, and achieve faster computational times.

The rapid growth of the Internet of Things has brought substantial benefits to our lives, along with substantial data storage and processing demands. IoT devices require substantial computational power and reliable energy sources, posing a significant challenge in modern networking systems. To address this, the Internet and telecommunications industry is transitioning toward 5G networks, which offer enhanced processing capabilities and near real-time energy harvesting. 5G networks' low latency also enables accurate slicing, crucial for IoT-based smart homes. To manage the energy sources of IoT devices in 5G networks, the Internet and telecommunications sector has proposed integrating renewable energy technologies such as solar and wind power generation. Our study proposes an innovative, blockchain-powered smart home system that utilizes 5G networks to monitor energy usage by solar and wind power through IoT-driven sensors, and managed by a blockchain-based ledger. Our research aims to optimize energy efficiency by leveraging the computational power of IoT devices, and our results demonstrate the potential of the proposed solution to meet the energy demands of modern 5G networks.

A deep learning model has been developed to address the issue of unbalanced P-CSI-RM usage in highly-circumferential zones with the ultimate goal of enhancing the accuracy of the L-value and reducing its entropy. Experimental results confirm the model's ability to achieve its objective, leading to verification of the quantization scheme's feasibility through both simulation and field trials. Furthermore, the application of the proposed quantization scheme yields a performance improvement of up to 1.5 dB compared to traditional QPSK modulation in both simulation and field trials protocols.

A polygonally-upward planar drawing of a graph features x- and y-coordinates for each vertex such that the x-coordinate increases with the vertex's index, while y-coordinates maintain strict increase for edges, assuming a standard x-axis. We've developed several new algorithms for recognizing and constructing an up-planar drawing for graphs, using parameterized methods based on specific graph characteristics. For example, we have created a novel algorithm that takes the input of a graph with bounded outerpath width and runs in time O*((gamma)^w), where gamma is the graph's maximum degree. We've also provided algorithms for chordal graphs and K-r-minor-free graphs (for small fixed values of r) that run in time (gamma^k), where k represents the respective graph parameter. Additionally, we have extended these methods to bipartite graphs through the use of a specific parameter.

The analysis of crowdsourced data, particularly that from data labeling tasks,
poses a unique challenge due to its inherent uncertainty and bias. Unlike
traditional datasets, many in these data labeling tasks are open-ended and
prone to errors, making them unsuitable for standard machine learning
approaches. This paper presents a novel analysis framework that effectively
utilizes such noisy, crowdsourced datasets. The proposed framework combines
ensemble modeling with human softmax distributions and entropic metrics of
uncertainty to extract meaningful insights from these datasets. This framework
can be applied to a wide range of datasets, from those in data labeling tasks
to open-ended surveys, and has the potential to improve the accuracy of
crowdsourced data by up to 20%.

For semiflows with rapid mixing properties, the exponential rate at which the transfer operator's norm diminishes in various $L^p$ spaces, where $p$ exceeds 1, is often surpassed by other semiflows in terms of other measurable quantities such as its $L^1$ variation or $H^{-1}$ norm. This diminished decay rate for $L^p$ norms ($p>1$) was previously illustrated in certain weak Gibbs-Markov maps of the Smale-Stephenson type on the interval.

This paper proposes a novel framework for minor strength-2 covering arrays, offering a more efficient solution compared to the existing minor strength-2 covering arrays. By generalizing the concept of minor coverage, the proposed framework allows for more flexible testing applications. It is demonstrated that the new covering arrays can be constructed using the Kronecker product and further simplified through a depth-reduction method, ultimately leading to the creation of minor strength-2 covering arrays with smaller dimensions.

Contests involving multiple parties over shared resources can be challenging due to their non-local nature. Research has analyzed such contests using non-local games, examining strategies that can be either mixed or deterministic. Our study focuses on contests that allow for noisy integration of parties and limited numbers of agents. Surprisingly, we found that under these circumstances, it is still possible to find a winning strategy, even if it requires searching through a vast number of possibilities. Specifically, we demonstrate that it is sufficient to look through a polynomial number of variables to either find a winning strategy or determine that none exists. To achieve this, we employ the Zeilberger algorithm to automate the search process and verify satisfaction using the Rybiak normal form. Our results not only expand upon previous findings but also switch the methodology for proving the complexity of certain contests from translation to search.

A recent paper by Malik et al., published in the Software: Practice and Experience journal in 2020, introduced a tool called CGA designed to replicate software failures automatically. However, due to the absence of relevant testing data from the original authors, we created a new test suite, leveraging issues from the Zephyr issue tracker and Fuchsia OS, to assess CGA's effectiveness in facilitating failure reproduction. A comprehensive study was conducted, utilizing various sampling methods and testing different subsets of the testing data, which allowed us to analyze CGA's performance in terms of multiple performance criteria. Unfortunately, CGA failed to meet its intended goals, as our results showed that it could not identify failing test cases consistently, often leading to false positives. Instead of streamlining failure reproduction, CGA often required testers to perform extensive, time-consuming manual work, including installing software and configuring test cases. Consequently, our study suggests revisiting the evaluation metrics used in the CGA paper, which may not be suitable for assessing failure reproduction tools. Furthermore, our test suite, though incomplete, could serve as a resource for evaluating other tools aimed at achieving various software testing objectives.

Theoretical predictions suggest a complex behavior of vortex dynamics in high-temperature cuprate superconductors, particularly a transition between triangular and square grids of vortices. Although this prediction aligns with basic Ginzburg-Landau theory, it remains experimentally unverified. In our study, we successfully observed a similar but modified transition in a doped cuprate, starting from the established square-shaped arrangement of vortices and undergoing a gradual change into a squared-based square-grid configuration.

Researchers investigated thermal photon production angles for very short time periods, typically less than 0.000000001 seconds, and discovered anisotropic flow signatures in the process. An unusual "V"-shaped pattern in the anisotropic flow of thermal photons was found, caused by the viscosity of the quark-gluon plasma. As a result, the measurement of the coefficient of viscosity through the analysis of thermal photon anisotropic flow offers a more sensitive and reliable approach than previously proposed methods, such as the correlation of electron-positron pairs and lepton pairs, and can potentially serve as a direct and reliable indicator of the early properties of the quark-gluon plasma.

Kagome lattices with magnetic properties, particularly in nearly kagome salts based on the 12Ni${}^{2+}$, 1S unit cell, have become a key platform for studying unique magnetic behaviors through controlled experiments and theoretical analysis. A recent investigation of the kagome lattice's consistent magnetic structure, focusing solely on in-plane interactions within a single honeycomb subgroup, has revealed significant results, with ten distinct ground states identified through computational methods. Notably, five of these states exhibit an equivalent energy and can be categorized into three distinct symmetries. The presence of specific bond configurations further distinguishes these ground states, offering potential control over the system's magnetic properties.

In large-scale intervention effect identification studies, multiple hypothesis tests are often used to compensate for the effects of noise and biases. The issue of dependent local tests has been resolved by the development of dependent localization rate control, allowing researchers to manage complex test dependency relationships. However, this method requires knowing the dependence structure, which is often unavailable. This paper proposes a novel, conservative method for controlling dependent post-test statistics that do not require knowledge of the dependence structure, and instead rely on regulated localization rate control, which can be estimated through statistical methods. The localization rate control approach outperforms the widely used Bonferroni correction, significantly reducing conservatism under regulated post-test conditions. Through extensive simulations and empirical analysis, the method was shown to provide accurate control over post-test statistics under localized post-test assumptions, offering better performance than the Bonferroni method.

I'm developing a custom indicator, the 'Astronomical Expansion,' based on log-periodic scaling laws to forecast stellar phenomena such as supernovae, white dwarfs, and nova explosions. By tracking periodic fluctuations in astronomical data over time, these laws help establish the timeframes for future stellar events.

The long-standing anomaly in the $-2$ muon anomaly $a_\mu$ in the Fermilab Muon $g-2$ experiment has persisted for over 80 years.  A considerable difference in the $W$ mass $m_W$ has also been identified at approximately $4-5\sigma$ from the Standard Model (SM) prediction and towards a higher $W$ mass.  A comparison of the $-2$ and $W$ mass discrepancies reveals that the Standard Model $-2$ value along with the measured $W$ mass are mutually exclusive at $5\sigma$ confidence, suggesting the potential involvement of new physics.  To address the $-2$ and $m_W$ discrepancies, we introduce the type-X 2HDM model, often referred to as the 2-2 model, which is widely used in explaining the flavour anomalies in $B$ meson decays.  A detailed examination of $-2$ and $m_W$ in the context of 2-2 model is presented, with specific attention paid to its impact on flavour observables such as the branching ratio of $B^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$, and the ratio of branching ratios $\mathcal{R}_K$ and $\mathcal{R}_P$.  By incorporating non-zero $\mathcal{CP}$ terms into dipole coefficients, our 2-2 model is capable of making predictions for

Current query rephrasing techniques rely heavily either on unsupervised methods using large corpora or on supervised models trained on carefully curated datasets created by professionals. Both approaches have limitations in addressing complex queries or achieving high accuracy rates. To bridge this gap, we developed SWIFTER, an automated query rephrasing system, designed to uncover new concepts in unstructured data. By integrating crowd-sourced input from workers, SWIFTER generates diverse query formulations, enhancing its performance. Evaluations across three real-world datasets demonstrate SWIFTER's success in generating accurate and diverse concepts, outperforming existing query rephrasing and concept discovery baselines by a significant margin of 10-20%.

This article's primary goal is to introduce a novel method for measuring synchronization in conversational speech. Unlike traditional approaches, our proposed technique relies on automatically extracting synchronization distance without the need for human-labeled data. We demonstrate that the problem can be addressed by a multilayer perceptron, which is capable of learning the required features from scratch. To facilitate this, we define a dataset consisting of speech pairs along with their semantic distances, which serves as a proxy for speech-based distances. The method's approach, the underlying assumptions, and its performance evaluation against a manual-annotated soccer commentary dataset are discussed and analyzed.

RCSEDv2 is a two-part Python library that facilitates the visualization and analysis of multi-wavelength imaging and spectral data. The repository includes ready-to-use online services: a figure creation tool for image stacking and spectroscopic data analysis, in addition to a chart creation tool for spectral data visualization and cross-correlation comparison. The RCSEDv2 toolset is currently being utilized in the SKA1-MID project, which is expected to produce an extensive amount of spectral data. The RCSEDv2 tools are designed to accommodate both single-spectrum and multi-spectrum analysis. The toolset is now available under an open-source license at https://rcsed.versionofinterest.github.io/RCSEDv2/.

Human action recognition, a crucial and challenging issue, is the focus of our proposed approach, termed Self-supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing (SSCAP). SSCAP employs a self-supervised framework, specifically utilizing the Temporal-Spatial Self-Attention (TSA) model, to achieve logical action recognition based on the principles of human action co-occurrence. By designing a comprehensive set of diverse and granular co-occurrence relations, SSCAP facilitates the development of temporal and semantic action recognition without relying heavily on annotated datasets. To further enhance performance, SSCAP incorporates the Loss of Reciprocal Consistency (LRC) for robust action discovery. SSCAP demonstrates superior performance on UCF101-24 and UCF101-20 datasets compared to other state-of-the-art approaches.

A novel pentaquark state of $B_{bs}$ has been predicted with a distinctive structure, notably its large mass and negative parity, making it suitable for creation in the $B$-meson decay process. A more massive $B_{bs}^*$ partner has positive parity and can potentially be produced through $B^{*}$ decays. These decays facilitate the formation of the pentaquark states, and their decays into $\bar{B}^{(*)}S$ are dominated by the quark-recombination amplitude, allowing for favorable detection via these resonances.

A common testing education approach, Code Review, often centers around students assessing flawed code by identifying and categorizing defects. We propose an innovative, student-driven method called Code Clues, which facilitates students providing general testing feedback, offering a simpler alternative to detailed evaluation methods currently used in industry and education. We conducted two studies to compare the efficacy of Code Clues against traditional techniques. We found that students using Code Clues discovered more defects than those employing traditional methods, suggesting that this method may be as effective, if not more so, for software testing education purposes. We discuss the benefits and limitations of Code Clues, along with the study's and this approach's potential applications.

To bridge the gap between theoretical models and practical applications, we're focusing on transferring knowledge from a theoretical source domain to a target domain with limited labels in the theoretical framework. Unlike traditional domain adaptation methods that focus on data distribution shifts, our approach recognizes a fundamental difference between the distribution shifts of theoretical and data domains, which renders those methods ineffective. We've developed a theory transfer framework, including a source-free adaptation method called SS-TT. This method employs a optimization-driven approach, where a small semi-supervised dataset is used to fine-tune the source model, and a method based on manifold structure is used to select the most representative subset of data for optimization, enhancing the source model's performance on the target domain with limited resources, computational constraints, and memory limitations.

Nuclear reactors serve as innovative alternatives to traditional chemical propellants for powering spacecraft and interplanetary missions. Research is currently focused on developing more powerful and efficient nuclear thermal and electric systems. This report examines the potential advantages of nuclear reactors that operate at very high temperatures and are designed with gas-core technology. These reactors have an increased specific impulse and operate at lower total mass compared to conventional nuclear systems. We propose a path forward for research into this type of nuclear reactor, which is suitable for remote space propulsion and space-based manufacturing.

Identifying the precise 3D location of interactions within astroparticle detectors is a crucial challenge, particularly when detecting neutrino-spark events like those occurring within the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment. To tackle this problem, we employ a domain-informed neural architecture known as the domain-informed neural network (DINN), which integrates knowledge-driven constraints derived from detector geometry and engineering specifications into the neural network's target function. Our initial evaluation of the method involves localizing interaction points within simulated neutrino-spark data within three distinct detector segments of the Fermi Lab's Near-Nu Detector. Notably, the method's core concept is universally applicable to various computational tasks, including but not limited to the described geospatial localization problem.

The research of substellar exoplanets involves the potential detection of atmospheric absorption features. However, existing databases for molecular absorption cross-sections lack accuracy for the temperatures, pressures, and metal abundances present in these atmospheres. Past studies relied on extrapolations of data obtained at lower temperatures and pressures, rather than empirical data from actual measurements. This research aims to address this gap by compiling absorption cross-sections for ten key molecules across a broad range of conditions spanning from 200 to 700 K and pressures up to 10 bar for each molecule. Ten brown dwarf and giant exoplanet atmospheres are modeled individually and supplied with corresponding absorption cross-sections, absorption coefficients, and transmission cross-sections at 0.6, 0.8, 0.65, 0.85, 0.43, 0.77, 0.2, 0.4, 1.4, and 2.2 microns. These datasets facilitate the analysis of atmospheric features in substastial giants through various observational techniques.

Grounding is a crucial step in answering symbolic queries through Answer Set Programming. It allows for the handling of undefined symbols by temporarily removing them from the knowledge base. Different grounding techniques vary in the symbols they retain for further processing, which affects the size of the resulting grounded program. While we cannot pinpoint a universal standard for optimization, we suggest guidelines based on the underlying programming paradigm and the specific requirements of the task, such as preserving variables, nested structures, or overall program groundness.

We introduce a framework of universal quantum resource theory centered on specifying desired resources. Within this, initial and final resources are pivotal, as they embody primary question marks and provide clear benchmarks, respectively. Our approach involves developing a general resource theory where every possible resource can be derived from these two fundamental ones. Notably, this methodology can be applied to multiple existing theories of quantum resource management, including entanglement, coherence, and steering, where specific, standard states serve as initial and final benchmarks.

We analyze how information in a sample of independent and identically distributed data can be summarized by three criteria: the efficiency of estimators, the tightness of bounds for functions of the population distribution, and the accuracy of approximations via polynomials. Our study integrates results from hypothesis testing, decision theory, and approximation theory to derive efficient estimators, precise bounds, and converging polynomial approximations that share a connection through the functional expansion of estimators and approximations about the population distribution. By leveraging functional expansions, we derive a single set of scores characterizing sample data, including a list of preferred moments, the stochastic process generated by these scores, and the rate of convergence for approximations. A data assessment scheme based on these scores facilitates the comparison of statistical procedures and the determination of the most valuable data features for a given task. Our analysis exemplifies this assessment with focus on the Chernick-Efron-Weisberg method for distribution approximation, but we also consider alternatives such as Gaussian approximation, polynomial approximation with other bases, series expansions with Legendre and Chebyshev polynomials, and universal approximation via neural networks.

We analyze the long-term patterns in complex, time-dependent data sequences that have a skewed distribution. Using a mathematical approach, we analyze a specific model of dependent random variables and examine a method of estimating their key statistical properties, such as a parameter that controls the severity of extreme events. A mathematical proof is given to show that this estimate is reliable in the long run. To assess the performance of this method, we use simulation and real-world data from the S&P 500 stock market to calculate the probability that multiple sequences will simultaneously exceed a certain threshold. Our research reveals that the mathematical model is highly sensitive to specific parameters, such as the severity index. To address this issue, we develop a new mathematical model by combining the original sequence with another set of independent random variables, such as those that have a uniform or normal distribution. We analyze the effects of adding these supplementary random variables on the mathematical model's behavior, such as its dependence structure. Our results show that the mathematical model becomes less sensitive to specific parameters, such as the severity index, when supplementary random variables are added.

Efficient channel codes based on low-density parity-check (LDPC) methods can offer optimal performance in the limit of large block sizes. A recent development has yielded LDPC codes with properties of infinite rate, finite relative distance, and finite dispersion for the Shor code. Nonetheless, conventional LDPC decoders, which operate using belief propagation and are often used for the Shor code, exhibit exponential time complexity. In contrast, our proposed quantum LDPC code family, specifically designed for the depolarizing channel and utilizing the petz recovery operator, exhibits linear time complexity in its interaction graph. Furthermore, systematic decoding processes have been devised to leverage quantum operations efficiently without consuming quantum memory.

In graph theory, a distance-$r$ controlling set ensures that every pair of vertices outside the set $S$ has a shortest path that intersects $S $. We demonstrate that for any integer $r\ge2$, a random set of size $O(n/r)$ can control all pairs in sparse graphs with high probability when the graph has a large girth number. We also explore an equivalent problem by showing that a small set of size $O(\log^2 n)$ ensures that all pairs have a path going through it, provided the graph has a minimum degree of 3. We plan to investigate the problem's NP-completeness and fixed-parameter tractability.

We have established an accurate analytical calculation for the average binding energy of impurity states near band edges in one-dimensional topological insulators and higher-order topological insulators in two and three dimensions. Our result for the average binding energy of intraband impurity states matches the specific dimensionality of impurity state wave functions to the power, validating previous numerical and experimental findings on the formation of extended states at the band edges in random dimerized chains and quadratic nodal point semimetallic materials, respectively. Furthermore, the derived bound state energy formula is validated by our own and external numerical data for various bond disorder types in the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model and in nodal point materials. Our research also covers the case of interband impurity states in dimerized chains, finding that their bound state behavior is notably influenced by the strength of the intraband coupling in strong disorder regimes.

Over the last decade, direct searches for supersymmetry at the LHC have not yielded any evidence for its existence. As a result, researchers have shifted focus towards indirect supersymmetry searches, aiming to refine their sensitive areas and refine their sensitive ranges. Given recent findings on the neutrino mass, we propose using neutrino oscillation data to set a new, well-constrained upper limit on $\alpha/\Lambda^2$, where $\alpha$ represents the fine structure constant, and $\chi$ denotes the neutrino contribution to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, $a_\mu$. We then explore a range of Supersymmetric models to identify viable areas in parameter space that can simultaneously satisfy current constraints on $\alpha$, $m_\tau$, and the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, $a_\mu$.

Our proposed approach employs deep simulation and rendering techniques to create a more efficient alternative to traditional transfer functions used in visualizing volumetric data. The framework, inspired by physics-based shading and rendering, uses neural networks to predict bright field images from unprocessed volumetric inputs. The data volume conditioning model conditions the prediction of these images using unprocessed volumetric data. The framework, which uses 3D convolutional neural networks, is trained on synthetic data without labeled pairs, leveraging self-supervision through identity loss, relative depth loss, and color normalization. The framework, which is relatively lightweight, demonstrates its efficiency by producing high-quality, detailed images while maintaining a low inference time of 10.3 milliseconds on modern hardware. The framework, which is suitable for clinical environments, has the potential to provide high-fidelity visualization without the need for manual transfer function design.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2021, involving SOAR/SPECKLE II and SOAR/MPCC instruments, yielded 146 successful datasets. The speckle imaging data collected enabled resolution measurements of 18 binary systems, with 15 new binaries being identified. Notably, 5 of these newly discovered systems were previously unknown, adding to the catalog of visual binary stars.

Chiral algebras offer an innovative way to connect two different methods of describing super-amplituades, specifically integrability and hidden symmetries. When chiral algebras are applied to heavenly sigma models, they reveal a new, four-dimensional chiral algebra, which extends an existing, four-dimensional algebra based on self-dual Yang-Mills theory. The model features Riemann curvature operators that serve as commutators, much like the Drinfeld-Sokolov reduction produces Gelfand-Dickey operators from Lax operators. Furthermore, the model demonstrates colour-kinematics equivalence, as its action exhibits required kinetic properties. Lastly, the model's operator product expansions create an integrable, parafermi conformal field theory, as the operators expand into integrable Green functions with kinematic poles, confirming the model's integrability.

A comprehensive study examines the changes in structure, polarization properties, and dynamics of a massive low-solar-coronal jet complex, which was captured using LOFAR at 168 and 248 MHz the same day as the event occurred. The complex, which was observed in a dense region near the equator of the Sun, is located at a height of about 8.5 times the solar radius above the surface. It was discovered that multiple bursts of non-thermal radio emission, with frequencies of 168 and 248 MHz and lasting 20-30 minutes, were triggered 15 minutes after the jet's peak speed, which was about 3,000 km/s. These bursts, which were circularly polarized, were positioned approximately 80,000 km in front of the dense solar-pilot cap, which was the site of the fastest acceleration of the jet.
