Our approach randomly selects matrix columns, and the efficiency of the method depends on whether there is a correlation between a column's singular values and the rank of its corresponding low-ramp matrix. Specifically, we can stop sampling once a certain "tensor tension" is reached, where it has been shown that the empirical rank accurately approximates the true rank beyond this point. This stochastic algorithm significantly outperforms existing techniques, and we further provide a rigorous proof of the first stochastic tensor SVD method with known bounds on the sampling required for accurate rank approximation.

As graphs continue to grow in representation, they are increasingly being used to capture dynamic data. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are capable of processing these evolving graphs by first converting them into fixed-dimensional vectors through embedding techniques. This work delves into various methods of embedding evolving graphs, focusing on their impact on dynamic data. Given that GNNs serve as the foundation for these approaches, this study also examines how GNNs work under the Neighbourhood Propagation and Spectral Theory perspectives. Furthermore, this analysis explores how different methods of capturing time-dependent information in evolving graphs can be achieved.

To identify the $^7$H nucleus's existence, we need to understand the properties of its ground state excitation. By linking the $^7$H ground state to the $^3$H and four neutrons, researchers have used the continuum shell model. This approach incorporates the effects of the $^3$H and $^4$n cluster continuum. The results indicate that the $^7$H ground state has a spin-parity of 7/2$^-$ and is highly unstable against the emission of $^3$H. The findings from the continuum shell model are in line with experimental data and can be used to interpret its mass-energy difference. The mass-energy difference of $^7$H is estimated based on the $^7$Li mass and the energy required to separate $^5$H and a two-neutron cluster.

This research paper examines the Dirichlet - Neumann boundary value problem for the nonlinear equation $-\Delta u = V(x)e^{2(n-1)u}e^{\beta u}$ defined on a half sphere, with boundary conditions set at $\beta u = Q^2$, where $V(x)$ is a positive, periodic function, and $\beta > 0$. We investigate the behavior of this problem for values of $Q$ approaching a critical threshold and demonstrate that under specific conditions on $V(x)$ and $\beta$, there exist sequences of blowing-up solutions that blow up at a finite point $x_0 \in \Omega$. These blowing-up sequences can exhibit a finite or infinite magnitude, and blow up points can occur at either an interior point or boundary of the domain $\Omega$. Moreover, in many cases, the blowing-up solutions behave similarly to the classical Yagi-type solution for the Laplace equation, despite variations in magnitude.

Recent advancements in deep representation learning have been significant, yet they
often rely on pre-defined task-specific knowledge or assumptions, and
consequently struggle to generalize effectively when faced with diverse and
unseen challenges.  This article proposes innovative deep representation
learning methods that demand minimal prior information and instead leverage
innovative applications of optimal transport theory.  Given a collection of
data distributions, the proposed techniques generate a single, universal
representation that enables efficient distributional classification by optimal
transport metrics, and consequently tackle various tasks simultaneously.
This strategy effectively learns deep representations without relying on
predefined assumptions or utilizing task-specific knowledge.  To showcase the
efficacy of this method, it surpasses existing approaches in image classification
and has shown considerable potential in classifying complex graph distributions.

In the UK's coronavirus contact tracing system, local authorities assumed responsibility for following up with high-risk individuals in certain areas. We investigated the impact of this varying approach by analyzing the 88 English local areas involved, focusing on two key time periods before and after March 2021. Our research indicates that the strategy to maintain contact tracing local control resulted in unequal and unpredictable data protection capabilities, particularly before March 2021 when it reduced effectiveness by 13% on average.

Researchers have analyzed the Gaia DR2 data to examine the open star cluster, Melotte 72, to gain insights into its composition. Their observations revealed a consistent and symmetric main sequence with a distinct turn-off point and a prominent main sequence gap. Star counts analysis yielded an estimated mass for a binary system within the cluster at 1.6 solar masses, and the derived distance from main sequence analysis was found to be 1.72 kpc. Interferometric measurements of four members aligned well with the data-driven proper motion analysis. Kinematic data indicated Melotte 72 belongs to the local thick disk population, and its turn-off point aligned with a disk cluster featuring a distinct main sequence feature. Furthermore, the data revealed Turn-Off Point Mass (TOPM) values across the sample to average 0.545 solar masses, with a consistent value for Melotte 72.

Inspired by Guo and Kurylev's findings on the stochastic structure of Gaussian fields, we examine the topological properties of a modified version called the Gaussian wandering, specifically in the dimensions of $0$ and $1$. To address this, we examine two scenarios: one where the wandering is defined over the standard standard Gaussian percolation model on a specific lattice and the other where the graph in question has degree that grows with its size. Our analysis shows that the Betti numbers of these fields grow exponentially with their size when the density is very low. Our results also reveal the influence of topology on the Betti numbers, while the method we employed to derive our analysis is general and applicable to a variety of similar field models.

Our approach efficiently calibrates the intrinsic parameters of an eye-in-hand robot camera from a lone image containing the service robot's front-facing pinhole camera. This method leverages the distinctive movement patterns of a human's gaze to produce a set of intrinsic parameters that closely replicate those of a human's eye. These 'human-eye-like' cameras excel at mimicking human vision, which in turn enables eye-in-hand cameras to achieve pinhole camera accuracy with minimal to no additional learning required. This remarkable self-calibration results in significant reductions in training data and time, which we attribute to the simpler, more predictable movements of a robot compared to those of a human. Experimental simulations further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed self-calibration method.

A common issue in robot learning is transferring off-wall contact forces to various environments. Reverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning (RCRL) enhances traditional Reinforcement Learning (RL) by incorporating a "reverse" optimization step that adjusts policy parameters. These parameters are used to maximize a goal-oriented value function, considering both contact force and navigation constraints, ensuring a consistent mapping of forces to controls. We demonstrate through evaluation that RCRL improves mapping consistency and achieves better sample efficiency in a simulation environment compared to RL. Moreover, our method's applicability extends to an online setting, where it can be used for planning in combination with Model Predictive Control (MPC). We validate this integration with a physical humanoid robot, showcasing its ability to recover from various perturbations.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission is set to significantly advance our understanding of the Galaxy and its star populations by making the most of its unprecedented photometric, astrometric, and spectroscopic capabilities. This mission will mark a pivotal moment in our comprehension of stellar astrophysics, astrophysical stellar populations, galactic astrometry, galactic archaeology, galactic evolution, and evolutionary stellar data. This comprehensive overview of GAIA's mission aims to provide an introduction to its goals, goals, and capabilities.

We present a novel algorithm, running in time O*(2^(tw^2*t^3 log tw)), that effectively reduces the number of a chosen treewidth bag's classes to two while maintaining the same treewidth. This achievement significantly outperforms previously established bounds, which were time O*(3^(tw^3,t^2,log tw)). Our approach leverages Courcelle's theorem, which, although yielding less optimal results, enables us to overcome earlier constraints. Compact vertex dividers have a wide range of applications, including the enhancement of parameterized complexity algorithms, modular graph algorithm design, and fixed-parameter tractable solvers for the maximum clique problem.

We examine the weighted grouping WGCn, a method that creates networks by assigning observations to communities based on their similarity in a lower-dimensional space. WGC facilitates complex data analysis with multiple related variables by allowing for flexible network construction. However, the method's complexity hinders understanding its alogarithms, limiting its effective application. This work aims to clarify the weighted grouping procedure, its implications, and the assumptions that underlie it. By doing so, we provide guidance on selecting an appropriate WGCn configuration and establish the boundaries of its applicability.

To ensure reliable decision-making, error estimation is a vital component in machine learning, allowing model developers to measure performance in areas they cannot directly validate. Our approach for estimating performance after training a machine learning model, authorized error estimation, is, essentially, reverse engineering of conventional Bayesian methods. This formal method is particularly suitable for validating neural network models that incorporate physical knowledge in their training. Our proposed solution is illustrated with a test problem involving heat transfer.

In epidemiological studies, air contamination models analyze the spatial-temporal distribution of airborne pathogens and other air pollutants. The assessment of air quality is crucial for making informed public health decisions and understanding the dispersion of pathogens and pollutants caused by human activities or natural events like wildfires and volcanic eruptions. Researchers typically employ two atmospheric dispersion models, receptor models and source inversion methods, to identify the influence of human and natural sources and predict the dispersion of contaminants. This review examines advancements in atmospheric dispersion research over the past five years, with a particular emphasis on the integration of geostatistical and artificial intelligence methods in air quality models, along with the use of machine learning for receptor modeling.

To differentiate between the coherence gap filling Majorana peak and other spectral peaks in density of states, a technique involving the conversion of a normal metal tip into a resistive system has been proposed for in situ tunneling spectroscopy of a Majorana wire. By regulating the coherence energy gap through the impedance in the metal tip, one can establish resonance conditions between the Majorana bound states and the environment, which results in residual spectral weight. This approach enables effective distinction between the coherence gap filling Majorana peak and other spectral peaks.

Linear contextual bandits, a crucial decision-making framework under uncertainty, have been proposed in various fields like recommendation systems and network information theory. Nevertheless, existing linear bandit models often fail to address diverse action sets, where different contexts have varying algorithmic choices due to technological limitations, input differences, or availability. To resolve this issue, a new learning framework called Linear Bandits with Diverse Action Sets (LDAS) has been introduced to generalize linear bandits for dynamic action sets. To effectively solve the LDAS problem, a novel learning approach called DIVA has been developed, which provides mathematical proof of its sublinear regret, demonstrating its optimality. Through computational experiments, DIVA's performance has been evaluated and found to surpass existing solutions like RegretHedge across multiple problem settings, highlighting the importance of modeling diverse action sets accurately in real-world applications, particularly network resource allocation.

Graphene with an energy gap that respects mirror symmetry serves as an ideal system for exhibiting a non-trivial Berry curvature in its valence and conduction bands, which can't be attributed to a valley-dependent curvature vector potential due to the absence of a well-defined valley Hall effect in massless Dirac fermions. However, when interacting with a weak electric field, these fermions can exhibit a novel response characterized by an orbital Hall effect, which differs from the Hall effect observed in charge conservation systems due to its lack of influence on the longitudinal current. Moreover, even a modest relaxation of the ideal Dirac spectrum can lead to an additional response driven by charge conservation, superimposing valley Hall effects onto the primary orbital Hall effect.

The success of graph neural networks (GNNs) heavily relies on high-quality graph data for training, yet their vulnerability to adversarial attacks has been overlooked in previous studies focusing primarily on machine learning models like decision trees and support vector machines. Graph data contamination attacks, which involve adding malicious graphs or modifying node/edge features to deceive GNNs, pose a significant threat to their performance. To tackle this, we developed an adaptive data contamerment model, which simulates an attack that adjusts its strategy in response to GNN responses during training. By doing so, we uncover GNNs' weaknesses to such attacks and compare our model's results to those of GNNs under both targeted and random attacks, ultimately demonstrating the effectiveness of our model in inducing adversarial samples that degrade GNN performance when applied to existing state-of-the-art GNNs.

The problem of matching celestial objects between different catalogs poses a unique challenge due to varying naming conventions, font styles, and resolutions, making automated verification difficult. In order to overcome these obstacles, we utilize spectroscopic and photometric data, specifically combining them in a unique way, to establish reliable mappings between catalogs of galaxies. Our approach, which involves processing spectral data, has shown promising results in matching galaxies, and now we extend this method by incorporating multi-band photometric data and accounting for the effect of stellar reddening. By training a deep learning model on galaxy spectra and photometric data, we achieve a high level of accuracy in object matching, matching or surpassing the performance of existing methods while reducing computational complexity. Our results show that a combination of photometric and spectral data is essential for accurate galaxy matching, especially when reddening effects are taken into account. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical applicability of our model on real-world datasets and showcase how it can be leveraged to study galaxy properties.

In the context of hypergraphs with a maximum vertex degree of $d$, a theorem proves the existence of edge sets of size $m$ that efficiently cover all edges when $m$ exceeds a certain threshold that depends solely on $d $. This theorem generalizes a discovery by Erd\H{o}s regarding graphs, and highlights a specific dependence on $d $ when the threshold is considered, H.  2 $ for graphs but increases to $d $!$ 2($d $ - 2)$ for $d $-hypergraphs.

Ontologies, expressed in languages like OWL, map concepts and their connections. They're crucial for data analysis and knowledge management applications. Traditionally, ontologies are displayed using graphs, but they often become too complex to understand due to their vast number of nodes and connections. To address this issue, OntoPlot, a new visualization tool, breaks down large ontologies into manageable sub-groups based on the frequency of their connections and common attributes. By doing so, OntoPlot enables users to explore and navigate within each subgroup, improving their overall understanding of the ontology.

This study investigates a semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) method, focusing on improving performance through cross-domain training. Two novel techniques, based on adversarial training and inter-domain penalty integration, are proposed. Experimentally implemented on two speech datasets, Speech5 and OpenSLR 10, the proposed methods demonstrate significant improvement over superset features and single-domain AS models.

A fundamental skill for mobile robots is autonomous navigation, which can be effectively learned through an intrinsic predictive system. This ability allows a robot to build an internal model of its surroundings and update it as new information becomes available. Although traditional navigation approaches rely on precise map data, less structured methods have shown promise in addressing the complexity of building and refining internal models through hypothesis testing. This research presents a new framework for autonomous navigation by adapting a hierarchical brain-based algorithm to fit mobile robots. This adaptation addresses key differences between brain activity and robot sensor data, which typically provide point-based information. This enhanced algorithm excels in scenarios with obstacles of non-zero dimensions and when integrating sensor data from dimmed images and limited depth readings. This enhanced algorithm excels in scenarios with obstacles of non-zero dimensions and when integrating sensor data from dimmed images and limited depth readings. This algorithm's success has been demonstrated in a series of navigation tests, which show improved performance compared to a baseline system based on a hierarchical brain-algorithm.

We develop a general theory for predicting the binary diffusion coefficients of flexible molecules in solution mixtures under a influence of a temperature gradient. The theory examines the impact of a solute molecule's flexibility and that of its surrounding solvent. Based on the assumption that internal movements are unimpeded, we create a mathematical framework based on the solution's density profile. Building upon the Chapman-Enskog approach for rigid-body molecules, we adapt it to accommodate flexible solutes. As a result, we find that increased freedom of movement for solutes leads to elevated barodiffusion coefficients, while decreasing the magnitude of the thermodiffusion coefficient. The increased solute flexibility weakens the size difference effect, resulting in smaller solute-solvent cross-interaction parameters. Conversely, limitations on solute internal freedom or solvent limitations reduce the magnitude of the thermodiffusion coefficient. The findings of our theory are supported by direct simulations of simplified fluid models for various temperature and density ranges, demonstrating the method's effectiveness in predicting the Soret coefficient of flexible solutes in solution.

Recent advancements in Input-Output Automatic Program Generation (APG) have demonstrated significant potential. Recent studies have focused on combining large language models with automated synthesis to enhance performance, which is a significant step forward. However, evaluating the accuracy of these models remains a significant hurdle, particularly since traditional output models are often inadequate. We have designed novel automated APG evaluation methods that leverage transformer-based large language models, specifically adapting and fine-tuning RoBERTa for this purpose. We initially formed synthetic instruction datasets and refined our approach using real-world APG tasks from the Arena Code Challenge, the LiveCode Benchmark, and the Haskell Compiler Construction Evaluation Suite. The results show that our weakly supervised approach, relying on human user feedback, performs on par with or surpasses stronger but fully supervised training on multiple APG evaluation benchmarks. Moreover, our approach provides more accurate and informative evaluation of APG models compared to traditional output models, offering more precise performance comparisons.

In practical situations, few-shot pedestrian identification often results in numerous false positives due to limited data. To address this issue, a novel approach known as box re-ranking has been proposed to reduce false positives without additional training. Although existing methods effectively re-rank predictions using detection boxes, they are typically applied in unsupervised environments and focus on reducing false positives by considering only the center point of bounding boxes. To further improve performance, a more refined model is suggested that takes into account the shape and size of boxes by utilizing three key features provided by a detector. This enhanced model can be combined with an existing method to update the detector's training objective and yields superior results, as demonstrated on several public datasets.

Conventional audio enhancement techniques, such as audio source separation and audio super-resolution, are limited by their reliance on limited datasets, pre-processing requirements, and pre-trained models. On the other hand, advanced speech-to-text models can transcribe poorly quality speech effectively, but they fall short in reconstructing speech with high fidelity. To overcome these limitations, a novel approach is introduced that transforms a low-quality audio clip into a color image and then encodes it to reconstruct a high-quality version. This method is built upon an innovative image conversion technique that preserves speaker characteristics and an image-to-speech vocoder to regenerate the reconstructed audio. Notably, only the vocoder needs to be trained on a comprehensive dataset of poorly quality audio pairs. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in handling a diverse range of distortions.

Our ability to throw objects accurately involves the correct timing of releasing them at a specific point in space, influenced by visual cues about the object's trajectory and flight time. Previous research has demonstrated that mistaking the point of release when watching others can lead to underestimating the distance traveled and the release distance in others. However, the effect of such errors on our own throwing movements has not been explored. Through three experiments, we investigated the impact of a manipulated point of release on our throwing movements, with results showing that a delayed release in one condition led to the maintenance of release distance integrity, with the point of release shifting further along the trajectory. Our findings suggest that the point of release is a crucial element in our throw-based actions, which aligns with the goal-directed model of throw-based actions.

Traditional syntax-based Natural Language Processing models are limited by the lack of ability to leverage top-down tree structures, which hinders their efficacy in tasks like translation and dependency parsing. To bridge this gap, a novel neural model is proposed, which integrates a tree structure trained independently with a seq2seq-based encoder-decoder translator, both equipped with syntax-aware cross-attention. This model's encoder, in conjunction with syntax-aware cross-attention, allows for the efficient exchange of information between the top-down tree and the translation task. To further connect the two components, a back translation approach is employed to align the training objectives. As a result, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on various metrics across multiple test sets in terms of translation accuracy and syntax-related evaluations, while also delivering a substantial boost to the standalone standi model's capabilities in dependency parsing.

A comprehensive distribution of binding energies is required for astrochemical models. To address this need, a online database, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform, has been established and provides binding energy distributions for 389 gas-phase molecules based on their frequency in the astrochemical community. Access to this database is accessible through a website and the data can be conveniently retrieved in ExoMol format for straightforward integration.

A well-known stochastic process, geometric brownian motion, is often used to model stock prices. However, the standard model doesn't account for a floor price below which a stock cannot drop. In response to this limitation, a new stochastic process has been developed that features a distinct phase transition when the floor value is involved. For a general minimum limit, the process shows convergence to this limit only for a sample size significantly larger than a critical threshold, $N_{c}$. Above this threshold, the distribution of process values around the minimum limit becomes approximately Gaussian. The existence of this phase transition has been demonstrated using two distinct analytical methods. Additionally, the paper outlines the steps for generating random data based on the new process and compares the resulting data to geometric brownian motion.

We utilize random Clifford circuits, including those with considerable depth, to draw the observer's attention toward crucial regions in a quantum state, and to facilitate the measurement of quantum shades in expectation. The effectiveness of our approach is confirmed through analysis of specific benchmark states, where the accuracy with which we can estimate quantum shades is directly linked to the depth of the Clifford circuits. Moreover, we discover that even Clifford circuits with low depth are capable of addressing complex states, including entropy-1 states, and estimating the correlations between adjacent qubits in MERA wavefunctions with minimal loss in precision. These findings suggest that shallow Clifford circuits possess valuable "quantum shade assessment capabilities."

The reflection coefficient's behavior at large $k$ varies significantly based on the results of orthogonal eigenfunctions associated with non homogeneous Cauchy problems, which can lead to different asymptotic patterns of growth or decay. In Davey-Stewartson II equations, a particular case arises where the reflection coefficient exhibits growth as $k$ increases, occurring when singularities in the joint spectral problem arise. This results in the reflection coefficient behaving like $k^{-\alpha}$, with $\alpha$ taking values between $-1$ and $0$.

This paper presents a text categorization method, text Sibylvariant categorization (TCC), which addresses the challenge of mitigating the negative effects of malicious data on machine learning-based systems. In this context, two types of adversarial inputs are considered: Sibyl vectors, a type of adversarial data that is specifically crafted to be misclassified, and anti-Sibyl vectors, a type of adversative data that is designed to correctly classify legitimate data. Two novel Sibylvariant-based methods have been developed: Sibylvariant K-SVM and Sibylvariant Adaptive One-SiMLP. These algorithms are designed to filter out malicious data from a dataset. In contrast to traditional Sibylvariant-based methods, such as Sibylvariant One-SiMLP and Sibylvariant K-SVM, which either overlook the relationship between malicious data classes or fail to recognize their anti-Sibyl vector counterparts, these proposed algorithms take this into account, resulting in enhanced performance. Comprehensive experiments conducted on different datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms, with their superior performance further validated by comparative studies.

We propose an innovative, meta-learning framework, which trains a drawing generator to create illustrative inputs in which the object of interest can be clearly identified with minimal ambiguity. Our goal is to develop a drawing technique that enables even a human to accurately interpret it. In the initial stage, we create a collection of reference images and use them to train a drawing generator with demonstrability as the primary objective. Next, we fine-tune this generator with hand-drawn inputs to enhance its drawing capabilities. Finally, we compare our method to existing image-based learning techniques in controlled, indoor, and outdoor settings, showing that our approach produces drawings that allow accurate interpretation under various noise conditions, outperforming direct, non-learning-based techniques, as well as comparable to state-of-the-art, non-meta-learning-based methods in the direct condition.

High-performance multilingual machine translation (MT) models are becoming
accessible through open-source platforms like HuggingFace, enabling language
technologists to utilize them. Nonetheless, these large models demand substantial
computational resources, hindering their deployment in developing regions.
Consequently, researchers are exploring methods to create low-resource models
leveraging the pre-trained, high-performance models. Two prominent approaches
are utilizing distilled models extracted from larger models or quantized versions,
both aiming to improve specific tasks through distillation. This research compares
their effectiveness by examining their stability under compression, focusing on
the consistency of both the main model and teacher-models during evaluation.
By employing this stability metric along with translation quality assessments,
the experiment reveals the limitations of quantization and extraction methods,
indicating that distillation offers only minimal improvement. Meanwhile, the
experiment suggests that quantization may be a more effective approach than
extracting smaller models, given the findings.

The N-body problem within the framework of hypergraph theory is revisited, specifically the case of an isolated system consisting of three elements. A new hypergraph Lagrangian is proposed to describe the motion of this system, but an examination of the resulting Euler-Lagrange equations reveals that they contain contradictory and nonsensical statements.

In the field of medical image segmentation, deep learning algorithms have achieved exceptional success in producing highly accurate predictions. The high accuracy comes with a significant trade-off of high computational costs and the necessity for vast amounts of labeled data to achieve optimal performance. To overcome these limitations, weakly supervised learning techniques, such as self-supervised learning, have been developed to reduce the amount of labeled data required and increase robustness to variations in data quality. This paper presents a method for pneumonia segmentation, where a supervised model is trained in conjunction with an unsupervised data enhancement network that improves its own predictions by generating enhanced images. This approach, known as supervised self-supervised learning, has been tested on a dataset of chest X-rays and demonstrated promising results, significantly decreasing the amount of labeled data required to achieve high accuracy, achieving 79% IoU with 1000 annotated images, compared to 67% IoU with 1000 annotated images using a standard supervised approach.

Media literacy is an essential skill in the modern world, emphasizing the importance of questioning information sources, especially in the context of image-based misinformation like deepfakes and manipulative photo editing. Current AI-powered image description systems, although helpful in assessing the veracity of misleading content, can't consider the varying information needs of different users, some of whom may prefer concise descriptions, while others may require detailed descriptions. This research introduces a novel approach to regulatable image description using a large language model, where users can control the level of detail in the description simply by specifying a desired level. Through a series of experiments and human evaluations on a newly developed dataset, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, offering a customizable and adaptable way to generate image descriptions tailored to users' preferences.

This paper explores the 'causal effect' between two entities, X and D, where X is a treatment variable and D is a random variable situated within a broader causal framework. Various conceptualizations of causal effect and their respective mathematical formulations in terms of distributions of U and Δ are examined. It is shown that these concepts diverge significantly from one another and carry distinct practical implications. As an instance of the causal understanding of causal effect, a causal difference variable is derived. This variable, Δ_U, is defined as a function of U, Δ, and the conditional distribution of D given X, where D^* represents a copy of D. The causal difference variable exhibits an advantage over traditional causal effect measures due to its direct observational estimation through D^*. Furthermore, this variable retains interpretability in terms of a population counterfactual and can be related to structural causal models.

Over the past few years, deep learning has become a widely used approach for resolving complex data analysis problems, yet it's typically time-consuming and demanding to train, making it essential to efficiently use data parallel computing resources. We are introducing MMLSpark/MMLDL, a unified framework that allows the seamless integration of deep learning and other machine learning algorithms in Pyspark on cloud computing platforms. This integration enables algorithms to be executed on a dynamic number of nodes, automatically adjusting to changes in the computational environment. As a result, algorithms can be trained on a varying number of nodes, with the capability to save models from multi-node training sessions for single-node predictions. The framework also supports the continuous addition of new learning algorithms and real-time model hyperparameter optimization using population-based methods. Furthermore, MMLDL framework provides an interface for deploying algorithms on edge computing devices and compatibility with cloud platforms such as Azure HDInsight, Azure Databricks, and Databricks on other cloud platforms.

Voice conversion tasks often require training with a diverse range of speaker voices and require significant computational resources, posing a significant challenge in developing Voice Conversion models. Our novel zero-shot voice conversion approach requires no training and instead leverages a pre-trained 3D-Campbell model to translate any two voice distributions without needing representative examples. This method effectively handles rare or previously unseen speaker pairs, demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional multi-speaker voice conversion methods through comprehensive evaluations. Our research showcases zero-shot voice conversion as a practical, versatile, and efficient tool for speaker conversion tasks.

This work focuses on the mathematical analysis of a model inspired by the work of Gurtin, which describes crystal growth. The study employs a system of PDEs coupled with algebraic equations to account for the thermodynamic equilibrium of a material. The equilibrium condition is expressed as a dynamic boundary constraint. The solution's existence and uniqueness over time are proven through a combination of methods: fixed-point theorem and rigorous estimates. The analytical findings rely heavily on the properties of parabolic equations and their associated positivity principles.

The integration of renewable energy technologies and smart devices within the low voltage grid has resulted in an increasingly unpredictable load profile. To mitigate this issue, a novel daily electricity consumption model combining historical data, weather conditions, and forecasted inputs has been developed. This model demonstrates the ability to accurately forecast low voltage network demand even in the absence of energy balance, making it an ideal tool for grid operators and distribution system managers. Furthermore, the model can identify the most probable source of high consumption by analyzing a three-day forecast incorporating weather and energy supply data.

The increasing popularity of machine learning has led to its widespread use in numerous fields. However, its applications are often limited by a lack of input from domain experts. This study aims to provide a comprehensive framework for incorporating domain expertise in machine learning models. A framework is presented, consisting of four key components: data, objective function, constraints, and confidence. A review of literature reveals 308 sources related to each component, which are further categorized into 26 subcategories. A framework of metagraphs is developed to support the creation of complex knowledge structures from the reviewed sources. Subcategories within the data and objective function components are explored using percolation theory, aiming to identify the most influential sources within each group. A practical example, modeling COVID-19 testing uncertainty using Bayesian methods, illustrates the proposed framework. Ultimately, this study serves as a foundational resource for researchers and engineers seeking to incorporate domain expertise into machine learning models, ultimately enhancing their performance and reliability.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have made COVID-19 lung lesion segmentation and localization a reality, but current methods are prone to bias and overfitting, which can be detrimental to generalization performance. To address this issue, our research proposes an innovative weakly-supervised learning framework that can be applied to various medical image analysis tasks. This framework involves training convolutional neural networks with rough annotations, and our approach for lung lesion segmentation is based on a multi-scale joint classification model. Furthermore, to mitigate the risk of the deep learning model overfitting to joint classification, we developed a novel loss function that jointly considers individual loss and pairwise loss, and analyzed its relationship to traditional supervision methods. Experimental results on two public COVID-19 datasets confirm the effectiveness of our proposed model, with notable improvements and the potential to be adapted to other medical image analysis tasks that rely on lung lesion localization and segmentation.

The automatic assessment of spinal curvature for Beden-Fischer (BFC) requires the precise identification of vertebrae along the spine's central axis. Current approaches, which rely on 2D image analysis from clinical scans, often struggle due to vertebrae overlap and pose challenges for deep learning-based methods, particularly in cases of degenerative spine conditions. Moreover, these methods typically necessitate expert supervision and high-quality, full-spine imaging. To address these issues, a novel, more robust approach is presented, combining 3/4 view synthesis, vertebral localization in 3D space using deep learning, central axis estimation through anatomically-informed optimization, and training on a limited set of cases with corresponding guidance. The integration of these components significantly reduces dependency on domain expertise and enables training on available data alone. The innovative design of the underlying deep learning model, which incorporates aligned vertebral localization modules, further contributes to enhanced feature extraction and correlation between adjacent vertebrae. The superiority of this approach is demonstrated through validation on a comprehensive benchmark dataset, the SpineGenesis.

Our study demonstrates that dynamic stabilization through vacuum oscillations can be observed via resonant electron scattering experiments involving ultrastrong coupling regimes between light and matter. By examining a typical superconducting transmon qubit strongly coupled to a cavity, we not only show how measurement outcomes can uncover the effects of vacuum oscillations, but also how the dynamical stabilization influences resonant electron scattering in the ultrastrong coupling regime. Furthermore, our investigation explores the possibility of directly observing dynamical stabilization via the Zeeman splitting of a spin attached to an ultrastrongly coupled cavity. These research opportunities hold significant potential for studying light-matter interactions under ultrastrong coupling regimes.

A cutting-edge elastic-actuated quadruped platform has been developed to demonstrate the potential of integrating elastic elements in actuators for improved locomotion compared to rigid designs. This platform integrates series elastic actuators within the Open Source Robot Controller framework and utilizes real-time, elastic actuation dynamics in its movement, which is facilitated by a customized whole-body control algorithm. This controller explicitly considers the compliance of its actuators and is enhanced through subject-specific parameterization. To address mounting constraints, the actuator configuration is optimized for compactness, resulting in a functioning quadruped design with unique features including in-body actuator placement and a customized transmission system. This integration allows for the consideration of compliance in whole-body control and is supported by unique actuator configurations, which is further illustrated through comparative experiments highlighting the potential of elastic-actuated versus rigid-actuated movement.

Our discussion revolves around the concept of operational distinguishability as well as the associated quantum diamond shape boundary boundary, which involves the total variational distance and its corresponding bounds. In the context of composite systems, the phenomenon of quantum irrelevance emerges, which asserts a lower limit to the distinguishability of combined systems, characterized by a non-zero minimum difference. To address this issue, we employ a variational approach in our investigation, ultimately providing new insights into this topic. Our results reveal that the quantum irrelevance effect is not an inherent property of a specific class of states, but rather a consequence of the way we measure distinguishability, with the associated bound being the H\"{o}lder exponent of the distinguishability bound.

This study explores various aspects of a small-scale reconnection process that occurs within electron-ion plasmas that don't conduct electricity, specifically examining reconnection speed, energy movement, electron dynamics, and properties of plasma waves at the site of reconnection. Utilizing two-dimensional computer simulations that don't conduct electricity, researchers discovered that a key parameter influencing recombination velocity is $\sqrt{m_i/m_e}S\sqrt{8\pi\gamma_e n_{si}B^2/m_e c^2}$, where $m_i$ and $m_e$ are masses of ions and electrons, $S$ is the $S$-parameter describing magnetic field strength, $n_{si}$ describes ion currents, and $\gamma_e$ describes electron pressure. This velocity greatly exceeds traditional resistive rates by factor of $\sqrt{m_i/m_e}S$. Furthermore, as this process progresses, the width of the current layer increases, the ion distribution changes, the site moves upward in direction of magnetic field, and electron dynamics significantly impact its behavior. These electrons also excite high-frequency waves within the magnetic environment.

The concept of intrinsic properties is ubiquitous in our visual perception, such as recognizing fashion items based on their attributes. While conventional approaches for visual retrieval using intrinsic properties are effective for prominent items, they often struggle with less familiar garments. This paper introduces a novel method for fashion image retrieval that leverages intrinsic characteristics of clothing, enabling the identification of similar garments among a vast collection of images. The proposed technique, which differs from traditional query expansion methods, is based on a domain-adversarial approach, effectively concealing intrinsic properties from the query. Additionally, it involves a feature-level manipulation method to modify embedded features, shifting them within the feature space to produce more relevant results. The framework's second-level mechanism leverages this manipulation to yield superior performance. The proposed method has demonstrated exceptional retrieval performance on two benchmark datasets.

The paper develops the dual gradient descent method to tackle ill-posed issues in linear spaces using a source condition in a dual space, which contrasts the usual approach that relies on the original space. It's demonstrated that the method's convergence rate is contingent on the interplay between the choice of dual space, the smoothness of the source, and the regularity of the problem's constraint. As an example, the article uses the Tikhonov regularisation method to solve ill-posed issues in dual spaces, employing entropy regularisation for problems with positive definite data and Hardy data (involving functions with square integrable derivatives) in particular. The method's performance is subsequently evaluated through numerical experiments that recover Hardy data.

Depth estimation from sparse light field data is hindered by issues suchas occlusions and inaccurate ray modeling, primarily affecting regions with
blocked viewpoints. In our approach, traditional light field depth estimation
is complemented by an additional component that is specifically trained to
recognize and adapt its predictions in areas with occlusions. As a result, final
depth estimates can be derived as weighted averages of outputs from both
components, with the weights determined dynamically based on uncertainty.
Our method demonstrates state-of-the-art results on the MVIID dataset and also
outperforms existing solutions on other popular depth estimation datasets.

Using the bilinear method, we show that the Fokas-Lenells equation admits two distinct solutions, represented by formulas. The process begins with constructing a solution in the form of a eigenfunction, which is then multiplied by an arbitrary constant to yield the first formula. Additionally, the interaction Poisson sum formula for particles is also derived.

Our actions align with Hessian gravity findings, confirming that our double field theory approach inherently leads to actions with non-Riemannian nature, demonstrating that this approach naturally employs generalized connections and metrics as fundamental components. We discover that these components come in two forms, one corresponding to an orthogonal generalized metric and the other to a generalized Kaluza-Klein metric, both of which are rooted in the same generalized metric up to a generalized Schur trick. Our analysis reveals that our constructed models exhibit higher derivatives, despite initially appearing as lower-derivative models. We verify general covariance under T-duality for models derived from Schur products and provide additional supporting arguments for superstring theories. We list potential avenues for further exploration.

In dense WiFi environments, users frequently struggle with poor or unstable WiFi connections and may need to select the most suitable access point from a list of available options provided by their network administrator, but existing WiFi technologies do not facilitate optimal access point selection for end-users, and this research explores the link between channel load measurements and access point selection and examines the load exchange protocol in the context of IEEE 802.11v roving and mobile WiFi networks to provide real-time access point selection and connection handover between access points and access points and access nodes and access points and access nodes and mobile WiFi networks. and this research presents an algorithm that uses channel load measurements and the load exchange protocol to provide real-time access point selection and this research demonstrates the effectiveness of the algorithm in providing real-time access point selection in dense WiFi environments.
